title: Medicine-Pediatrics Residency
level: Clinical physician residency (combined Internal Medicine-Pediatrics; adult + pediatric)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Physician learner with prior medical-school-level anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology and pharmacology; intended for advanced learner/refresher use, not a prerequisite pathway.
Basic clinical epidemiology, biostatistics, physical examination and ethical handling of protected health information.
Learner should be able to interpret evidence under supervision; this course does not confer patient-care privileges.
objectives: Integrate adult and pediatric internal medicine reasoning while identifying age-specific differences and uncertainty.
Map clinical problems to current ABIM and ABP public content outlines.
Select and interpret diagnostic tests in context, explicitly considering pretest probability and risk.
Use current prevention schedules and growth/development resources with date/version checks.
Plan safe adult-pediatric transitions and communicate an actionable handoff.
Recognize emergencies requiring prompt supervised escalation.
Distinguish programme accreditation and board eligibility from online course completion.

units.title: Foundations, clinical reasoning and prevention
objectives: Construct problem representations that combine acuity, age, history and social context.
Choose screening/prevention steps using current recommendations and explain diagnostic test limitations.
Use shared decisions, ethical communication and safety-netting across a longitudinal relationship.
boardDomains: ABIM Internal Medicine detailed content outline
units.casePractice: Work through a fictional case prompt; do not copy patient records or clinical images. Use a linked authentic educational source only for guided comparison.
units.assessment: For unit 1, submit a one-page age-sensitive problem representation, differential and next-step rationale; score against accuracy 40%, reasoning 30%, safety/uncertainty 20%, communication/citations 10%. Include a note on what evidence is missing.

assignment.title: Dual-life-stage clinical reasoning portfolio
assignment.instructions: Create 4 fictional cases spanning infant, school-age, adolescent/young adult and older adult; for each, make an age-sensitive problem representation, differential, test rationale, safety net, and transition/follow-up plan. Cite current guidelines; do not use real patient data or reproduce images.

assessment.format: Original 10-item formative MCQ set plus 12 unit checks, written case portfolio and self-audit mapped to both public board outlines.
assessment.passingStandard: No validated pass threshold; use completion as a study checkpoint only, not predictor of board success.
assessment.feedback: Rationales cite public board and clinical sources. Recheck time-sensitive content before use.

studyHours.allocation: 76.5353 observed video hours plus 18 hours source reading, 12 hours case/assignment work, 6 hours retrieval practice and 7.4647 hours review = 120 suggested learner hours; plan only, not a measured workload or training equivalence.

medical.boardStatus: Two distinct component-board certifications/exams are available; there is no separate Med-Peds board examination. Board examination eligibility is conditional on successful completion of an ACGME-accredited combined programme and each board’s current individual requirements. The exact accreditation status of the two named offerings was not independently queried in the live ACGME program search.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent self-study course does not confer board eligibility. ABIM/ABP state Med-Peds is an integrated four-year pathway, ordinarily 24 months per discipline under ACGME requirements; confirm current accreditation, training completion, licensure and individual eligibility directly with ACGME, ABIM and ABP.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 58-year-old with diabetes has nausea, deep respirations, glucose 480 mg/dL and elevated anion gap. Which next step best frames safe initial assessment?

options.text: Assume isolated DKA and give a fixed insulin dose
Assess volume/perfusion, potassium, ketones, acid-base status and precipitant before protocolized treatment
Start bicarbonate for every low pH
Discharge after glucose falls

practiceQuestions.rationale: Evaluate severity and potassium/volume status and identify precipitant before treatment; exact therapy requires current institutional protocol and clinician oversight.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult with acute dyspnea, hypotension and unilateral leg swelling is being assessed. Which reasoning approach is strongest?

options.text: A normal oxygen saturation excludes pulmonary embolism
Estimate pretest probability, assess instability and use validated testing pathway; do not use D-dimer indiscriminately
Start anticoagulation in every patient with dyspnea
Chest radiograph alone rules out PE

practiceQuestions.rationale: Diagnostic test selection depends on pretest probability and hemodynamic status; unstable patients require urgent supervised clinical assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with cough, wheeze and retractions presents to urgent care. What best structures initial assessment?

options.text: Weight the finding and age-specific work of breathing, oxygenation, hydration and danger signs before narrowing etiology
Treat every wheeze as bacterial pneumonia
Use adult respiratory rate thresholds unchanged
Skip history if wheezing is audible

practiceQuestions.rationale: Age-specific physiology and severity assessment precede diagnosis; wheeze has a broad differential and no single finding establishes cause.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 4-year-old plots at the 8th weight percentile with preserved height velocity and no prior plotted measurements. What is the most accurate interpretation?

options.text: This alone diagnoses malnutrition
A percentile is a single diagnostic threshold
Plot accurately, review trajectory and context; charts support but do not independently diagnose
Do not use growth charts after age 2

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC states growth charts contribute to an overall clinical impression and are not stand-alone diagnostic tools.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 7-month-old is overdue for several vaccines. What is the safest educational answer?

options.text: Restart every series from dose one
Use the current age-appropriate catch-up schedule and check indications, intervals, precautions and addenda
Use the 2018 schedule because it is familiar
Give every vaccine at the same visit without reviewing contraindications

practiceQuestions.rationale: Use the current official schedule, catch-up table, indication table, notes and precautions; CDC page reports its posted 2025 schedule status as court-qualified.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with fever, hypotension and suspected infection is deteriorating. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Delay escalation until all cultures return
Recognize possible shock, urgently escalate, assess perfusion and follow local sepsis protocol
Give oral fluids only
Assume hypotension is benign if fever is present

practiceQuestions.rationale: Possible shock requires prompt supervised escalation and time-sensitive assessment; the course does not authorize treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with prolonged fever, conjunctival injection, mucosal changes and rash is discussed in a teaching case. Which is the key reasoning caution?

options.text: A constellation supports a differential and timely expert evaluation; no single symptom confirms Kawasaki disease
Rash alone proves it
Normal early tests always exclude it
Treat as routine viral URI without follow-up

practiceQuestions.rationale: Clinical criteria and timing must be integrated; urgent clinician assessment is needed, and educational vignette does not establish a diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: During transition planning for a young adult with childhood-onset chronic illness, what is the best practice?

options.text: Transfer records only after the 18th birthday
Begin developmentally appropriate, longitudinal preparation and confirm adult-care linkage, medication/insurance and patient self-management needs
Assume pediatric and adult teams share records automatically
Make transition a one-visit administrative event

practiceQuestions.rationale: Transition is a planned process; integrate readiness, continuity and practical system barriers. ACGME supports longitudinal training and continuity but does not prescribe independent real-world management.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 67-year-old with confusion has a sodium of 119 mmol/L. Which is most important initially?

options.text: Presume chronicity and correct rapidly
Assess symptoms, acuity, volume/etiology and urgent risk; correction must be carefully controlled under current guidance
Ignore the result if glucose is normal
Give free water empirically

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hyponatremia risks and correction depend on acuity, symptoms and cause; unsafe rapid correction is harmful. Apply current local guidance with supervision.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 13-year-old with a new seizure has returned to baseline. Which answer best reflects board-level clinical reasoning?

options.text: One episode proves epilepsy
Characterize event, immediate safety, provoking factors and neurologic/metabolic red flags; plan evaluation using age-appropriate guidance
Order every available test before history
Reassure without considering first-seizure red flags

practiceQuestions.rationale: Distinguish seizure from mimics, assess acute causes and red flags, then select evaluation; educational course is not a clinical disposition tool.

title: Child Neurology Residency
prerequisites: Medical-school-level anatomy, physiology, neuroscience, pediatrics and adult neurology; intended for advanced learners, not unsupervised patient care.
Baseline knowledge of neurologic examination, evidence appraisal and developmental milestones.
For board blueprint preparation, use the official current ABPN and ABP documents; this course is not an eligibility assessment.
objectives: Localize neurologic dysfunction across age groups using history and neurologic examination.
Classify seizures and episodic events using current terminology and explicit uncertainty.
Interpret diagnostic testing and evidence in context, including limitations and artifacts.
Develop broad differentials across epilepsy, headache, development, neuromuscular, genetic, vascular, infectious, inflammatory, oncologic, movement, sleep and behavioral domains.
Communicate family-centered, safe, ethical, evidence-qualified reasoning.

units.title: Foundations: localization, development, and pediatric examination
objectives: Use age-aware developmental history and neurologic examination to localize dysfunction.
Distinguish developmental variation from regression and urgent red flags.
topics: Neuroanatomy; developmental milestones; mental status, cranial nerves, tone, reflexes, gait; exam adaptation by age.
units.casePractice: Analyze a fictional infant exam; submit a localization map and a justified next-step differential
units.assessment: Analyze a fictional infant exam; submit a localization map and a justified next-step differential. Rubric: localization 40%, age/context 25%, differential 20%, safety/communication 15%.

units.title: Seizure classification, epilepsy syndromes, and EEG reasoning
objectives: Describe events with precise semiology and classify onset using current ILAE terminology.
Integrate age, EEG, history and imaging without treating a single test as diagnostic in isolation.
topics: Focal/generalized/unknown onset; neonatal seizures; electroclinical syndromes; EEG artifacts and limitations; genetic/developmental epilepsy.
units.casePractice: Classify three fictional event descriptions and state evidence that could change classification
units.assessment: Classify three fictional event descriptions and state evidence that could change classification. Rubric: terminology 30%, data integration 30%, uncertainty 20%, alternatives 20%.

units.title: Acute seizures and status epilepticus
objectives: Sequence stabilization, seizure recognition and timely escalation conceptually.
Compare evidence strength and avoid inappropriate certainty about second-line drug superiority.
topics: Convulsive status; nonconvulsive status recognition; rescue planning; cardiorespiratory risks; EEG escalation; etiology.
units.casePractice: Create a time-ordered teaching algorithm using guideline qualifiers, not patient-specific orders
units.assessment: Create a time-ordered teaching algorithm using guideline qualifiers, not patient-specific orders. Rubric: sequence 35%, evidence qualifiers 30%, safety 25%, citations 10%.

units.title: Headache and paroxysmal non-epileptic events
objectives: Separate primary headache patterns from secondary-headache warning features.
Build a differential for common episodic behaviors, including non-epileptic events.
topics: Migraine, tension-type and secondary headache; tics; syncope; sleep-related and infant paroxysmal events; interview/video history ethics.
units.casePractice: Write a fictional triage reasoning note for headache and a separate event classification note
units.assessment: Write a fictional triage reasoning note for headache and a separate event classification note. Rubric: red flags 35%, differential 30%, reasoning 25%, safety 10%.

units.title: Neurodevelopment, cognition, autism, and behavior
objectives: Interpret developmental trajectory and functional impact across domains.
Select evidence-informed assessment/referral pathways and communicate uncertainty respectfully.
topics: Surveillance versus screening; regression; language/motor/cognitive development; autism; ADHD/behavior; school and family context.
units.casePractice: Map a fictional developmental history to domains, differential and referral questions
units.assessment: Map a fictional developmental history to domains, differential and referral questions. Rubric: developmental synthesis 35%, differential 25%, family-centered communication 25%, sources 15%.

units.title: Neuromuscular, hypotonia, and motor-unit localization
objectives: Localize weakness/hypotonia to brain, cord, nerve, NMJ or muscle using exam patterns.
Choose appropriate diagnostic categories and recognize urgent respiratory/bulbar concerns.
topics: Floppy infant; motor milestones; reflexes; motor neuron disease, neuropathy, NMJ, myopathy; CK/genetic testing concepts; respiratory red flags.
units.casePractice: Complete a fictional localization matrix for infant hypotonia
units.assessment: Complete a fictional localization matrix for infant hypotonia. Rubric: localization 40%, differential 30%, test rationale 20%, safety 10%.

units.title: Neurogenetics and metabolic neurology
objectives: Recognize clues to genetic/metabolic etiologies and inheritance patterns.
Use a phenotype-first strategy and explain test limits and counseling boundaries.
topics: Developmental epileptic encephalopathies; leukodystrophy/metabolic clues; neurocutaneous disorders; variant interpretation; genetic counseling referral.
units.casePractice: Construct a fictional phenotype-to-test decision tree
units.assessment: Construct a fictional phenotype-to-test decision tree. Rubric: phenotype extraction 30%, differential 25%, test limitations 25%, ethical communication 20%.

units.title: Neuroinfectious, inflammatory, and demyelinating disease
objectives: Distinguish infectious, postinfectious, inflammatory and demyelinating presentations.
Identify urgency and frame CSF/imaging/serologic testing with appropriate caveats.
topics: Meningitis/encephalitis; autoimmune encephalitis; pediatric MS/demyelination; CNS vasculitis; differential with metabolic/infectious mimics.
units.casePractice: Submit a fictional differential with evidence thresholds and emergency considerations
units.assessment: Submit a fictional differential with evidence thresholds and emergency considerations. Rubric: differential 35%, test reasoning 30%, urgency 20%, uncertainty 15%.

units.title: Pediatric stroke, trauma, spinal and neuro-ophthalmologic presentations
objectives: Localize acute focal findings and identify vascular/traumatic/spinal differential categories.
Explain age-specific risk factors and urgent evaluation principles without protocol substitution.
topics: Arterial ischemic stroke, hemorrhage, cerebral venous thrombosis, trauma, spinal cord syndromes, raised ICP, visual/ocular motor findings.
units.casePractice: Present a fictional localization and differential at a case conference
units.assessment: Present a fictional localization and differential at a case conference. Rubric: localization 35%, differential 30%, safety 20%, citations 15%.

units.title: Neuro-oncology, movement, sleep, autonomic, and pain
objectives: Recognize common presenting patterns and construct differential diagnoses across less frequent domains.
Account for age, medication effects and multisystem context.
topics: Pediatric CNS tumors; paroxysmal and chronic movement disorders; sleep disorders; autonomic dysfunction; neuropathic/central pain.
units.casePractice: Build a one-page symptom-to-localization comparison chart
units.assessment: Build a one-page symptom-to-localization comparison chart. Rubric: coverage 35%, discriminating features 30%, medication/safety 20%, references 15%.

units.title: Diagnostic procedures, imaging, EEG, CSF, and evidence appraisal
objectives: Interpret the purpose and limitations of EEG, imaging, CSF and neurophysiology tests.
Use sensitivity/specificity and pretest probability to avoid over-reading incidental findings.
topics: EEG sampling/artifacts; MRI/CT rationale; age-aware sedation considerations; CSF interpretation; EMG/NCS; genetics; evidence hierarchy.
units.casePractice: Appraise a fictional test panel and identify at least two alternative interpretations
units.assessment: Appraise a fictional test panel and identify at least two alternative interpretations. Rubric: test limits 35%, integration 30%, uncertainty 20%, safety 15%.

units.title: Longitudinal care, systems, communication, ethics, and transition
objectives: Integrate family-centered communication, disability rights and shared decisions into neurologic care.
Describe coordination, safety, transitions and professional duties across settings.
topics: Communication; privacy/consent/assent; equity; school and community systems; transitions; quality improvement; research ethics; multidisciplinary care.
units.casePractice: Create a fictional multidisciplinary handoff and quality-improvement question
units.assessment: Create a fictional multidisciplinary handoff and quality-improvement question. Rubric: clarity 25%, safety 25%, ethics/equity 25%, measurable improvement 25%.

assignment.title: Longitudinal fictional-case portfolio
tasks: Write an age-aware localization and developmental summary from a wholly fictional vignette.
Produce a seizure/event classification and evidence-limited diagnostic plan.
Submit a systems-oriented family communication/handoff and a critical appraisal of one cited clinical source.
assignment.rubric: Score each component 0–4 for accuracy, reasoning, age/context, uncertainty/safety, and source use (20 points each). Formative only; no clinical competency, certification, or eligibility inference.
assignment.safety: No patient records, identifiable details, copied images, medication orders or procedural instruction.

assessment.formative: Ten original board-style MCQs with source-based rationales, unit case analyses, retrieval quizzes and source appraisal.
assessment.summative: Portfolio rubric plus learner reflection identifying knowledge gaps and current guideline checks.
assessment.limitations: Not official board content, validated examination simulation, clinical assessment, or predictor of board passing.

studyHours.plan: Self-study plan, not measured video hours: 12 units x 5–7 hours of reading, note-making and assignments = 60–84 hours, plus the video curriculum goal of 36 hours. Actual time varies; this is transparently a planning estimate, never counted as video.

unitMap.text: Neuroinfectious, inflammatory, and demyelinating disease

coveredTopics: Pediatric CNS tumors; paroxysmal and chronic movement disorders; sleep disorders; autonomic dysfunction; neuropathic/central pain.

coveredTopics: Communication; privacy/consent/assent; equity; school and community systems; transitions; quality improvement; research ethics; multidisciplinary care.

topicGaps: Observed external public recording ledger contains 14 unique eligible videos (52225 seconds = 14.506944 hours); 21.493056 verified hours remain below the 36-hour target. Planned scripts/targets and self-study hours are not rendered or verified video.

The 40% adult-neurology share in the ABPN blueprint remains incompletely supported: added general-neurology recordings touch multiple domains, but there is no complete adult-neurology course, and several pediatric-specific differences are not taught in those recordings.

Insufficient recording coverage remains for pediatric acute stroke/vascular and spinal/trauma reasoning, neonatal neurology, EEG/CSF/imaging test interpretation, and systematic development/behavior/autism assessment.

Neurogenetic and metabolic topics are only partially covered; recordings do not constitute comprehensive phenotype, biochemical localization, or variant-interpretation teaching. Neuroinfectious, neuroimmune, and demyelinating videos are primarily broad/adult neurology and need child-specific sourcing.
Longitudinal pain, psychiatry, communication/assent, disability rights, systems-based practice, transition, and ethics lack sufficient specialty teaching recordings.

CHOP course duration is still unverified and registration is required; Utah examination demonstrations still lack a verified per-clip duration ledger. Neither is counted. A recording page being free-to-view does not convey republication or patient-image rights.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN): Neurology with Special Qualification in Child Neurology initial certification examination
American Board of Pediatrics (ABP): General Pediatrics Certifying Examination (conditional ABP–ABPN pediatrics-neurology pathway after qualifying supervised training)
medical.boardStatus: ABPN publishes a distinct initial Child Neurology certification examination. Its December 15, 2025 content specifications describe one 400-question exam titled Certification Examination in Neurology with Special Qualification in Child Neurology (60% child neurology, 40% adult neurology). ABP separately offers a conditional General Pediatrics certification examination pathway for candidates completing specified accredited pediatrics and child-neurology training. Neurodevelopmental Disabilities is a different pathway/field, not a synonym. A generic directory category does not create a separate board.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent self-study curriculum does not confer exam eligibility. Check current ABPN and ABP requirements and obtain official verification of accredited training. No pass guarantee.

topicGaps: Observed external public recording ledger contains 14 unique eligible videos (52225 seconds = 14.506944 hours); 21.493056 verified hours remain below the 36-hour target. Planned scripts/targets and self-study hours are not rendered or verified video.

The 40% adult-neurology share in the ABPN blueprint remains incompletely supported: added general-neurology recordings touch multiple domains, but there is no complete adult-neurology course, and several pediatric-specific differences are not taught in those recordings.

Insufficient recording coverage remains for pediatric acute stroke/vascular and spinal/trauma reasoning, neonatal neurology, EEG/CSF/imaging test interpretation, and systematic development/behavior/autism assessment.

Neurogenetic and metabolic topics are only partially covered; recordings do not constitute comprehensive phenotype, biochemical localization, or variant-interpretation teaching. Neuroinfectious, neuroimmune, and demyelinating videos are primarily broad/adult neurology and need child-specific sourcing.
Longitudinal pain, psychiatry, communication/assent, disability rights, systems-based practice, transition, and ethics lack sufficient specialty teaching recordings.

CHOP course duration is still unverified and registration is required; Utah examination demonstrations still lack a verified per-clip duration ledger. Neither is counted. A recording page being free-to-view does not convey republication or patient-image rights.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a fictional toddler with a convulsive event lasting 6 minutes, which broad initial medication class is supported by the 2016 AES evidence guideline once first aid/stabilization is underway?

options.text: Benzodiazepine
Oral maintenance antiseizure medicine
Empiric antibiotic only
No treatment until EEG

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline supports benzodiazepines as initial therapy for convulsive status at the operational 5-minute point; its evidence and local protocol caveats must be retained.

practiceQuestions.stem: An event description does not establish whether onset was focal or generalized. What is the best classification approach?

options.text: Force a focal label based on age
Use an uncertainty category and gather further semiology/EEG context
Diagnose epilepsy from one event description
Use “complex partial” without explanation

practiceQuestions.rationale: ILAE classification supports standardized terminology; uncertainty should be represented rather than inventing onset.

practiceQuestions.stem: A developmental history shows loss of previously acquired words and motor skills. Which framing is most appropriate?

options.text: Routine variation with no follow-up
Developmental regression requiring prompt clinical assessment of cause
Autism diagnosis is certain
Only speech delay is relevant

practiceQuestions.rationale: Regression is a clinically important trajectory change; surveillance resources do not diagnose cause.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which source has the strongest authority for the ABPN child neurology certification examination blueprint?

options.text: A hospital residency website
ABPN content specifications
A social media post
A local course completion certificate

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABPN publishes its own exam outline; a training institution page does not establish exam content or eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the board-exam relationship described for child neurology in the ABPN specifications?

options.text: Separate pediatric and child-neurology exams both administered by ABPN
One ABPN initial exam in Neurology with Special Qualification in Child Neurology
No certification exam exists
Only an ACGME exam

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABPN document names one examination and reports a 60% child/40% adult content split; ABP general pediatrics certification is a distinct conditional pathway.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is following an ACGME child-neurology program. Which statement reflects the published 2025 requirement?

options.text: The child neurology educational program segment is 36 months
All 5 years are adult neurology
No outpatient child neurology is required
Training is exclusively didactic

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 reformatted ACGME requirements specify a 36-month child neurology program component and required clinical/didactic experiences.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with hypotonia has weak antigravity movement and absent reflexes. What is the most defensible first reasoning step?

options.text: Assign a molecular diagnosis immediately
Localize the findings and broaden differential across motor unit levels
Assume normal variation
Select a treatment from an online video

practiceQuestions.rationale: Localization precedes etiologic certainty; exam demonstrations aid learning but do not substitute for examination or supervision.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 2021 CHOP seminar is listed as free and available. What should a learner know before relying on it?

options.text: All information is guaranteed current
CHOP explicitly says the lecture may contain information that has since been updated
Free viewing permits rehosting
It establishes residency eligibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: The course page states its age and warns of possible updates; copyright remains reserved.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best characterizes Utah’s Pediatric NeuroLogic Examination resource?

options.text: An official board exam
An educational tutorial with developmental-age demonstrations and linked copyright/reuse terms
A complete residency rotation
A source of patient charts to copy

practiceQuestions.rationale: The University resource describes 145 demonstrations across developmental ages; viewing is distinct from permission to redistribute.

practiceQuestions.stem: An online 2016 guideline suggests options for second-line status treatment. What should the learner do?

options.text: Treat it as timeless definitive instruction
Note its publication/evidence limits and check newer guidance and local protocols
Convert its tables into patient orders
Assume every medication has equal evidence

practiceQuestions.rationale: Guidelines are time-bounded and evidence qualifiers matter; the AES paper itself describes limits and was published in 2016.

title: Internal Medicine/Medical Genetics Residency
level: Combined clinical physician residency (Internal Medicine + Medical Genetics and Genomics)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Advanced postgraduate physician board-preparation/self-study; learners should already possess an MD/DO (or equivalent) and broad internal-medicine knowledge. This course is not entry-level medical education.
assumedKnowledge: adult internal medicine foundations and diagnostic reasoning

objectives: Map a clinical phenotype and family history to a prioritized differential without treating a single finding as pathognomonic.
Choose among cytogenetic, molecular, exome/genome and biochemical tests based on indication and limitations.
Explain variant classification, case-level causality, segregation, penetrance and uncertainty.
Integrate relevant common adult internal-medicine domains with genetic mechanisms.
Counsel about reproductive risk, secondary findings, privacy, equity and implications for relatives.
Interpret and communicate results using current clinical sources and appropriate specialist collaboration.

units.title: Mechanisms of inheritance, family history, pedigree, Bayesian risk
objectives: Draw a three-generation pedigree
distinguish AD/AR/X-linked/mitochondrial, de novo, mosaic and multifactorial patterns

assignment.title: Longitudinal fictional integrated case portfolio
assignment.instructions: Complete four linked written submissions: phenotype and three-generation pedigree; test-selection memo; structured variant interpretation with evidence limitations; patient-facing result and family follow-up explanation. Use only fictional scenarios in this file or lawfully linked public records. Cite dated board/guideline sources. No real patient records, images or copied proprietary exam items.

rubric.excellent: Concise, phenotype-led, includes competing diagnoses and red flags; distinguishes established facts from assumptions.
Justifies test and explains diagnostic scope, blind spots, confirmatory steps and alternatives.
Uses five-tier terminology appropriately; separates variant classification from patient-level causality; handles discordance.
Clear, non-directive, privacy-aware explanation; family and consent implications handled with uncertainty.

rubric.criterion: Source quality, date and safety boundaries
rubric.excellent: Cites current authoritative primary guidance, distinguishes examination blueprints from ACGME requirements and institutional pages, avoids unsupported treatment advice.

assignment.safety: Educational exercise, not real patient advice; no learner-directed therapy or procedure authorization.

assessment.format: Original formative retrieval checks, short structured consult memos, variant-evidence tables, and a capstone synthesis.

assessment.feedback: Require explanation of why distractors fail and a dated source check for treatment/testing claims.

unitMap.text: Mechanisms of inheritance, family history, pedigree, Bayesian risk
Clinical genetics consultation: phenotype-first reasoning
Genomic testing methods, test selection and result interpretation
Dysmorphology, congenital anomalies, neurodevelopment and multisystem disease
Variant classification, evidence integration and uncertainty communication
Pharmacogenomics and precision prescribing
Reproductive, prenatal and newborn genomics
Cancer genetics and inherited risk
Inborn errors of metabolism, neuromuscular and rare disorders
Internal medicine board domains in a genetics-aware practice
Ethics, consent, privacy, equity, and communication
Evidence synthesis, longitudinal care and board-style integration

topicGaps: The verified external-video ledger remains 13.36 hours; three newly linked, relevant recordings have public transcripts but their total player runtimes were not exposed, so they remain uncounted. The actual 36-hour floor gap is 22.64 hours; planned script minutes are not rendered video hours.

The broad 2026 ABIM adult internal-medicine blueprint is not covered comprehensively by the available genetics-heavy external video set; cardiology, endocrine, GI, infectious disease, renal, pulmonary, hematology, rheumatology, psychiatry, prevention, and other domains need current, independent study.
Current variant interpretation, assay/laboratory workflow, evidence conflict resolution, and equity/generalizability need more current instructional material than historical videos provide.
Reproductive genetics, cancer predisposition, inborn errors, counseling, bioethics, population genetics, and test limitations remain unevenly covered by directly verified-duration free videos.
Pharmacogenomic recommendations and gene-specific therapies are dynamic; historical recordings cannot substitute for current CPIC/FDA/guideline and product-label review.

The newly added NHGRI reproductive/cancer and EVMS internist recordings have transcript-end timing only; exact video runtimes and the complete duration of playback remain unverified, and the items are explicitly excluded from the hours calculation.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Combined clinical physician residency (Internal Medicine + Medical Genetics and Genomics)
boardNames: American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) — Internal Medicine
American Board of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ABMGG) — Clinical Genetics and Genomics
medical.boardStatus: Two distinct board certifications and examinations are available through the approved combined-training pathway: ABIM Internal Medicine and ABMGG Clinical Genetics and Genomics. This is not one combined exam. Actual eligibility depends on completion of approved/accredited training, board rules, licensure and other conditions. ABIM states combined training is 4 years/48 months and that, beginning 2025, an ACGME-accredited combined program is required for ABIM training eligibility; this deliverable did not independently confirm BWH’s present accreditation listing.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Self-study curriculum only. It does not establish ACGME training, qualify a learner for either board, grant licensure or guarantee certification. Confirm current ACGME status and individual eligibility directly with ACGME, ABIM and ABMGG.

officialProgrammes.institution: Brigham and Women’s Hospital
officialProgrammes.name: Internal Medicine/Medical Genetics Residency (BWH Combined Residency in Genetics and Medicine)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official BWH page describes a component of its Internal Medicine Residency intended to train selected IM housestaff in Internal Medicine and Medical Genetics; it says participants must already be accepted into BWH IM and be completing categorical PGY-1, with combined training beginning in PGY-2. It does not publish a full rotation map, didactic inventory, case volume or hours in the page reviewed.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The exact item packet identifies one official BWH institutional variant. It is a combined clinical physician residency, not a generic directory category or research-only postdoctoral role. The BWH page says physician/physician-scientist aims; that research aim does not convert the track into non-physician research training. No separate non-physician or research supplement is included. Johns Hopkins appears as a collaborator in an NHGRI lecture series, not as an institutional variant of this BWH combined residency. No other institutional variant is asserted.
sourceCaveats: BWH public programme page states aims and recruitment sequence but omits rotation schedule, actual didactics, resident case volume and specific total lecture hours. Do not infer these from ACGME standards.

ABMGG and ABIM describe a joint dual-certification pathway, with separate board rules/examinations. ABIM’s 2025 accreditation condition is not proof of BWH’s current status; query ACGME public finder and boards for live status.
ABMGG Clinical Blueprint effective August 2025 and ABIM Internal Medicine Blueprint dated January 2026 are exam-domain documents, not curricula or endorsements of this independent course.

Much of the accessible long-form specialty video material is dated 2011–2013. Count runtimes only; never rely on those recordings for current drug labels, screening protocols or therapy indications without a current source check.
One search-result-suggested course video labelled “Medical Genetics National Pre-Clinical Revision Course” redirected to unrelated advertising during page fetch; excluded.
The public GeneReviews index triggered a bot-check page in stateless fetch; linked for lawful reading but not claimed as fully fetched during this run.
Public video playback is counted, not permission to download/rehost. NHGRI pages identify CC BY reuse on several videos, but no content is reproduced here.

The actual 36-hour floor gap is 22.64 hours; planned script minutes are not rendered video hours.

The broad 2026 ABIM adult internal-medicine blueprint is not covered comprehensively by the available genetics-heavy external video set; cardiology, endocrine, GI, infectious disease, renal, pulmonary, hematology, rheumatology, psychiatry, prevention, and other domains need current, independent study.
Current variant interpretation, assay/laboratory workflow, evidence conflict resolution, and equity/generalizability need more current instructional material than historical videos provide.
Reproductive genetics, cancer predisposition, inborn errors, counseling, bioethics, population genetics, and test limitations remain unevenly covered by directly verified-duration free videos.
Pharmacogenomic recommendations and gene-specific therapies are dynamic; historical recordings cannot substitute for current CPIC/FDA/guideline and product-label review.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 34-year-old with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has an affected parent and affected maternal aunt. What is the best first step before ordering a broad panel?

options.text: Order a focused pedigree and obtain the relative’s records/known test result
Order consumer polygenic risk testing
Assume autosomal dominant with complete penetrance
Sequence the unaffected spouse only

practiceQuestions.rationale: A three-generation pedigree and informative family records establish phenotype, inheritance clues and whether targeted familial-variant testing is available. Inheritance cannot be presumed from this limited history; variable penetrance and phenocopies remain possible.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient’s exome report lists a variant of uncertain significance in a gene compatible with one symptom. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: Treat as molecular confirmation
Use the VUS alone to initiate irreversible management
Do not use the VUS alone for clinical decisions; assess phenotype and evidence and pursue appropriate follow-up
Classify it as benign because it is uncertain

practiceQuestions.rationale: A VUS is not a definitive result and should not be used by itself in clinical decision-making. The phenotype and full variant evidence should be reviewed; follow-up can include segregation or reanalysis as clinically appropriate.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has congenital anomalies and intellectual disability with a nondiagnostic initial evaluation. Which statement about ES/GS is supported by the ACMG guideline?

options.text: ES/GS should never be used until all single genes are tested
Consider ES/GS as a first- or second-tier test in the guideline-defined pediatric CA/DD/ID population
A negative genome excludes genetic disease
ES/GS replaces clinical evaluation

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACMG strongly recommends considering ES/GS as a first- or second-tier test for pediatric patients with congenital anomalies or DD/ID within the guideline’s defined age groups; negative testing does not exclude all genetic etiologies.

practiceQuestions.stem: A laboratory report has discordant pathogenic and benign classification submissions for a variant. What is the best response?

options.text: Select the most recent submission without review
Assume ClinVar independently adjudicates all submissions
Review the underlying evidence, submitter review status, phenotype fit and current lab interpretation; obtain genetics expertise
Use the majority vote as diagnostic

practiceQuestions.rationale: ClinVar is a freely accessible archive aggregating submitted variation classifications and supporting evidence; NIH does not independently verify submitter assertions. Reconcile evidence rather than treating database aggregation as a clinical adjudication.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient is considering a prenatal cell-free DNA screen for aneuploidy. What must be emphasized?

options.text: A positive screen is a definitive fetal diagnosis
A negative screen excludes all chromosomal and monogenic disease
It is a screening result; discuss residual risk and confirmatory diagnostic options in context
It is equivalent to fetal karyotyping

practiceQuestions.rationale: Screening and diagnostic testing are distinct. A screening result changes probability but is not itself a definitive diagnosis; options and limits should be discussed with appropriate clinicians and current guidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: A broad hereditary cancer panel finds a pathogenic germline variant in a patient with cancer. Which next step best reflects clinical genetics practice?

options.text: Equate the germline finding with the tumor’s complete biology
Discuss implications and family cascade evaluation, with current gene-specific guidance and consent
Assume all relatives carry the variant
Infer the variant from tumor sequencing alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: Germline findings can affect patient and family risk assessment, but require gene-specific interpretation, counseling, and appropriate testing of relatives. Tumor somatic findings and germline status are not interchangeable.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient taking a medication asks whether a genotype should alter dose. The only educational source is a 2012 lecture. What is the safest answer?

options.text: Follow that lecture verbatim
Check current drug label and a current pharmacogenomic guideline and consider clinical context
Change the prescription based on ancestry
Order a panel and change the dose before seeing results

practiceQuestions.rationale: Older lectures can teach mechanisms but recommendations change. Any prescribing decision must use current authoritative guideline/label sources and an appropriate clinical decision process.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has episodic vomiting, altered mental status and a possible inborn error of metabolism. What principle is most appropriate?

options.text: Wait for a genetic panel before any medical evaluation
Recognize potential urgency, involve the treating team/metabolic specialist and pursue appropriate biochemical and confirmatory testing
Assume all symptoms are explained by one VUS
Start a disease-specific therapy from a web search

practiceQuestions.rationale: Potential metabolic decompensation is time-sensitive. Clinical stabilization and urgent specialty evaluation take precedence; testing should match the suspected pathway and must not delay care.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult with no symptoms asks to use a direct-to-consumer result to decide whether to stop cancer screening. Best response?

options.text: Stop screening if the report is negative
Use the report as a medical diagnosis
Explain assay/context limits, obtain clinical confirmation when appropriate, and follow established screening guidance
Test the patient’s child instead

practiceQuestions.rationale: Direct-to-consumer data require careful contextual interpretation. They cannot safely replace clinical evaluation or population/gene-specific screening guidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: A counselor identifies a likely de novo variant in a parent and child, but the child’s phenotype is only partly concordant. Which reasoning is best?

options.text: Pathogenicity category alone proves causality
Evaluate phenotype fit, inheritance/segregation, technical validity and alternative diagnoses; explain residual uncertainty
Assume all discordant findings are incidental
Stop follow-up because the result is likely pathogenic

practiceQuestions.rationale: Variant classification and case-level causality are distinct. A likely pathogenic classification contributes evidence but does not by itself establish that it explains every clinical finding.

title: Combined Adult-Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Residency

prerequisites.audience: Advanced medical and postgraduate self-study; learners are assumed to have foundational biomedical science, general clinical reasoning, introductory psychiatry and professional ethics. Not entry-to-practice training.

objectives: Organize child/adolescent psychiatric assessment around developmental history, symptoms, function, informants, culture and medical context.

Explain evidence-supported treatment options, risks, uncertainty, measurement and monitoring at a knowledge level without prescribing for real patients.
Conduct safe fictional educational case discussion with confidentiality, consent, image-rights and supervision limits made explicit.
Map the institutional combined pathway separately from ABPN Psychiatry and CAP requirements and avoid eligibility claims.

topicGaps: Observed free public recording ledger totals 7.5572 unique hours across 7 videos; core specialty recordings total 6.2317 h and one explicitly supplemental recording adds 1.3256 h. These are observed runtimes, not viewing-time estimates.

Target remains 36 hours. Residual gap is 28.4428 h on all qualifying external recordings and 29.7683 h against core specialty recordings alone. No plan minutes, scripts, reading time, assignments, or inaccessible/unknown-duration candidates were counted.

Blueprint-wide gaps remain in full-length instruction for developmental assessment, interview/formulation, neurodevelopmental differential and comorbidities, anxiety/OCD/trauma, mood/psychosis, disruptive behavior and substance use, eating-disorder medical interface, medication safety, psychotherapy, emergency/safeguarding/ethics, and transition/equity systems. Individual recordings only supplement selected segments; no full publicly available CAP didactic curriculum was located.

Three previously reviewed candidates remain uncounted: two have no verifiable runtime/free access, and the newly checked youth-transition recording had an observed runtime but the direct watch page displayed “Video unavailable.” The adult-oriented psychedelic addiction lecture is only a supplement, not evidence for pediatric efficacy, indication or authorization.

The packet’s retained 32 one-hour original-clip production targets and five authored episodes are plans/scripts only, not videos. Actual feasibility is conditional on future production, clinician review, current-source verification, accessibility and lawful publishing; source gaps and the 36-hour shortfall remain.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

ABPN Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Certification Examination
medical.boardStatus: Psychiatry is an ABPN primary specialty certification; Child and Adolescent Psychiatry is a separate ABPN subspecialty certification with its own examination. This item is the MGH/McLean institutional Peds/Adult/Child pathway, not a generic ABPN combined-board category.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Do not infer board eligibility from programme name, NRMP code, or this curriculum. ABPN pages reviewed 2026-10-07 say usual CAP candidates must be ABPN-certified in Psychiatry by the deadline specified for the CAP exam, complete two full years/24 calendar months of CAP training, and satisfy other current requirements; Psychiatry primary certification has its own PGY-1 plus post-PGY-1 training, outpatient continuity and clinical skills requirements. Confirm a specific trainee’s route, current ACGME programme status, accepted PGY-1, training credit and exact eligibility with ABPN and programme leadership. Current public evidence does not establish MGH/McLean’s ACGME accreditation status as a combined programme. No eligibility is promised.

officialProgrammes.institution: McLean Hospital / Massachusetts General Hospital (Mass General Brigham; Harvard Medical School affiliates)
officialProgrammes.name: Combined Adult-Child & Adolescent Program (Peds/Adult/Child Psychiatry; NRMP 1261400C0)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official institution page: five- or six-year route, with MGH pediatric internship (six months pediatrics, one month adult neurology, four months psychiatry); then two or three years adult psychiatry before CAP training. The PGY-3 choice determines 5/6-year timing. The same page separately describes standard four-year adult psychiatry followed by a CAP fellowship and a fast-track alternative. It does not publish all didactics, exact required cases/hours, board eligibility confirmation or current combined-program accreditation evidence.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The exact name/5-or-6-year integrated route comes from McLean/MGH’s programme page. This was verified as an actual physician training path, not simply a generic directory category, non-physician supplement or research-only appointment. The institution page additionally lists distinct conventional/fast-track pathways. ACGME/ABPN policy pages establish general national requirements, but a live programme-specific public accreditation/board roster record was not verified statelessly. The ABPN separately recognizes Psychiatry and CAP examinations; integrated training route does not itself prove automatic dual certification.
sourceCaveats: Institution/program and board/ACGME sources answer different questions; institutional offerings are not proof of accreditation or board eligibility.
ABPN content outlines and eligibility pages are current as observed 2026-10-07; exam dates/deadlines, rules and effective accreditation documents can change. Recheck official pages before use.
The ACGME site linked psychiatry and CAP 2026 requirements effective July 1, 2026, but the extracted evidence did not show a programme-specific McLean combined accreditation record.
Some AACAP student-educator files are from 2009–2014 or member-only; use current authoritative guidance for clinical claims and respect link-specific permissions.
IACAPAP 2.0 account registration is required on the access page as of review; the free legacy version 1 is linked through December 2026. Chapter-specific license terms govern reuse.
Free-to-view recordings and case reports are not blanket republication licenses. No video, patient record, or diagnostic image has been copied into this course.
No human clinical review has been performed. All cases drafted for assignments/questions/scripts are explicitly fictional; they are not real patient records or claims about patient volumes.
Original plans are not ready videos; no generated media URL or estimated duration is represented as recorded.
This course grants no institutional affiliation, accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, procedure competence, certification or guarantee of passing any examination.

sourceReferences.claimSupported: As updated September 2025, ACGME resumed accreditation of combined programs from July 2025; ABPN only continues approving PPP pathways. This policy does not establish MGH/McLean programme-specific accreditation.

sourceReferences.title: ACGME Psychiatry Requirements, FAQs and Applications
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Current psychiatry and CAP requirements link and effective dates; requirements are standards for accredited training programmes, not a public curriculum or board blueprint.

sourceReferences.title: ABPN Psychiatry Certification Content Specifications
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Primary psychiatry certification content domains used as a mapping reference; version available via current ABPN page.

sourceReferences.title: ABPN CAP Certification Content Specifications
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Current subspecialty certification content domains used as a mapping reference.

sourceReferences.title: AACAP Practice Guidelines, Updates, and Parameters
sourceReferences.claimSupported: AACAP notes legacy Practice Parameters are discontinued and links current guidelines/resources; use current guideline pages rather than assuming old parameter is current.

sourceReferences.title: AACAP Clinical Practice Guideline for Major and Persistent Depressive Disorders in Children and Adolescents
sourceReferences.claimSupported: 2023 AACAP CPG supports systematic assessment, formulations, and treatment decision-making; CBT/IPT and SSRIs have empirical support as treatment options; clinical evaluation and individual care required.

sourceReferences.title: IACAPAP JM Rey's eTextbook access page
sourceReferences.claimSupported: IACAPAP version 2 is live but requires account registration; first edition remains available during the transition through December 2026. Access and license restrictions must be respected.

sourceReferences.title: IACAPAP eTextbook Version 1 chapter index
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Publicly linked free chapters across CAP topics; chapter-level licence governs reuse. Link/reading only, not republish.

sourceReferences.title: NIMH Child and Adolescent Mental Health
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Public NIMH developmental warning-sign information, help links, featured topics, and public-domain text policy; images remain excluded from reuse.

sourceReferences.title: NIMH Suicide Prevention
sourceReferences.claimSupported: NIMH public suicide-prevention information; supports safety and help-seeking teaching, not individual risk prediction.

sourceReferences.title: NIMH ADHD
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Public information on ADHD; educational background, not substitute for AAP/AACAP practice guidance.

sourceReferences.title: NIMH Autism Spectrum Disorder
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Public autism information and support; background only.

sourceReferences.title: CDC Developmental Milestones
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Developmental surveillance resources and milestone checklists; not a diagnostic test or substitute for comprehensive assessment.

sourceReferences.title: AACAP Resources for Medical Student Educators
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Teaching tools and links (some member-only, 2012–2014 resources, and third-party rights); free view does not convey reuse permission.

sourceReferences.title: Adolescent Depression: An Interactive Case-Based Session for Medical Students
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Open full-text educational case-based session with a constructed teaching vignette, assessment objectives and role-play. Original source material remains under article rights/license; link and cite; do not copy/rehost appendices without verifying license.

sourceReferences.title: AACAP 2026 Clinical Case Conference instructions
sourceReferences.claimSupported: AACAP says case information must be de-identified or family consent obtained; establishes ethical handling expectations, not a public clinical-record repository.

sourceReferences.title: Case Report: A Case of Pediatric Catatonia
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Publicly indexed published case report can support case reasoning by link only; authors/journal retain rights; exact de-identification/consent details must be checked in the article before reuse; do not copy images or patient records.

sourceReferences.title: Family-Centered Care in Adolescent Intensive Outpatient Program
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Open article includes a case-study discussion of a six-week adolescent IOP course; educational access is not a grant to copy or republish patient narrative; link and cite.

sourceReferences.title: Deprescribing Best Practices in Child & Adolescent Psychiatry (Wynne Morgan, MD)
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Public UMass Chan Psychiatry & Behavioral Sciences Grand Rounds recording; the watch page showed duration 56:21, title and public full-video option.

sourceReferences.title: An Introduction to Autism and the Autism Spectrum (Fred Volkmar, MD)
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Public Yale University recording from its Autism Center of Excellence; watch page showed duration 45:23 and public full-video option.

sourceReferences.title: Common Causes and Treatments of Depression in Children and Adolescents
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Public Stanford CME recording; watch page showed duration 1:15:46 and free full-video playback, with optional CME information linked separately.

sourceReferences.title: Webinar: Prescribing Psychotropic Medications for Pediatricians
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Public Florida Program for Behavioral Health Improvement and Solutions webinar; watch page showed 59:02 and public full-video option; primary-care framing, for critical review only.

sourceReferences.title: Eating Disorders in Children and Adolescents (Jennifer Derenne, MD)
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Public UMass Chan Psychiatry & Behavioral Sciences Grand Rounds; watch page showed 59:49 and public full-video option.

sourceReferences.title: AAP Clinical Practice Guideline: ADHD in Children and Adolescents (Wolraich et al., 2019)
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Primary-source KAS statements: evaluate ages 4 through 17 with relevant academic/behavior concerns; diagnosis requires DSM criteria, symptoms and impairment in more than one major setting, multiple informants, and ruling out alternatives; screen common comorbidities; treatment and monitoring differ by age and require clinical context. This is pediatric primary-care guidance, not a CAP board blueprint.

sourceReferences.title: AACAP Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Treatment of Children and Adolescents With Anxiety Disorders (Walter et al., 2020)
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Full guideline states CBT and SSRIs have empirical support as short-term options; evidence on long-term effects, comparisons and suicide risk remains limited. This is not patient-specific treatment advice.

sourceReferences.title: Seattle Children’s Psychiatry Grand Rounds video library
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Official hospital video-library entries list direct public video links, dates, titles and observed runtimes for Beyond the Handoff (01:18:08), Parental Mentalization (01:17:33), and Psychedelics for Substance Use Disorders (01:19:32). Archive runtimes are distinguished from planned event lengths.

sourceReferences.title: Beyond the Handoff: Strengthening Transitions to Adult Health Systems for Youth with Medical/Behavioral Health Needs
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Public Seattle Children’s recording, direct player runtime 1:18:07, describing transition to adult care for youth with complex physical and mental/behavioral health needs; supports systems/transition exposure but is not a universal transition protocol.

sourceReferences.title: Parental Mentalization (Helena Rutherford, PhD)
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Public Seattle Children’s Grand Rounds recording on parental mentalization and perinatal parent/child research. The speaker identifies the work as research and says she is not clinically trained; it is contextual exposure, not a diagnostic tool or clinical guideline.

sourceReferences.title: Psychedelics for Substance Use Disorders: A Primer for Providers (Nathan Sackett, MD, MS)
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Public Seattle Children’s Grand Rounds research lecture on emerging psychedelic addiction-treatment research, safety and hype. It expressly discusses investigational agents and does not establish pediatric treatment efficacy or authorization.

originalClipPlan.note: Production plan only; no recording exists or is counted. Episode length is a production target, not observed runtime.

topicGaps: Observed free public recording ledger totals 7.5572 unique hours across 7 videos; core specialty recordings total 6.2317 h and one explicitly supplemental recording adds 1.3256 h. These are observed runtimes, not viewing-time estimates.

Target remains 36 hours. Residual gap is 28.4428 h on all qualifying external recordings and 29.7683 h against core specialty recordings alone. No plan minutes, scripts, reading time, assignments, or inaccessible/unknown-duration candidates were counted.

Blueprint-wide gaps remain in full-length instruction for developmental assessment, interview/formulation, neurodevelopmental differential and comorbidities, anxiety/OCD/trauma, mood/psychosis, disruptive behavior and substance use, eating-disorder medical interface, medication safety, psychotherapy, emergency/safeguarding/ethics, and transition/equity systems. Individual recordings only supplement selected segments; no full publicly available CAP didactic curriculum was located.

Three previously reviewed candidates remain uncounted: two have no verifiable runtime/free access, and the newly checked youth-transition recording had an observed runtime but the direct watch page displayed “Video unavailable.” The adult-oriented psychedelic addiction lecture is only a supplement, not evidence for pediatric efficacy, indication or authorization.

The packet’s retained 32 one-hour original-clip production targets and five authored episodes are plans/scripts only, not videos. Actual feasibility is conditional on future production, clinician review, current-source verification, accessibility and lawful publishing; source gaps and the 36-hour shortfall remain.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 14-year-old is described as “lazy and oppositional” after a school transfer. Which next step best supports developmentally informed assessment?

options.text: Diagnose conduct disorder from the parent’s description.
Establish chronology, function across settings, the youth’s account, school context, developmental history, and relevant safety/medical factors.
Use an adult depression scale as the sole diagnostic test.
Assume the behavior is normative because it followed a transfer.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A formulation needs development, context, impairment, multiple perspectives, and differential evidence; one informant label or single screen cannot establish diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A screening scale is above its suggested threshold. What conclusion is justified?

options.text: The diagnosis is established.
The screen identifies a need for appropriate follow-up assessment; it is not a stand-alone diagnosis.
Treatment should begin without an interview.
No collateral information is needed.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Screening supports case-finding and measurement but diagnosis requires clinical evaluation, context, impairment and differential assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adolescent describes low mood and reduced activity for several weeks. Which additional line of assessment is essential before closing the formulation?

options.text: Ask only whether the parent agrees.
Assess suicide/self-harm directly, along with symptoms, impairment, timeline, differential contributors and possible past elevated-energy episodes.
Assume a depressive disorder because symptoms lasted weeks.
Avoid discussing suicide unless the adolescent raises it.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Comprehensive assessment includes symptom and functional characterization, safety, differential contributors, and possible bipolar-spectrum history.

practiceQuestions.stem: What does the ABPN page require for initial Child and Adolescent Psychiatry subspecialty certification in the usual U.S. pathway?

options.text: A free online course certificate.
Psychiatry board certification by the specified prior deadline, two full years of CAP training meeting ABPN rules, and other requirements including the subspecialty examination.
Only an institutional combined-track title.
A single general psychiatry examination with no CAP exam.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPN describes CAP as a psychiatry subspecialty with a separate certification exam and stated training/credential requirements. Program-specific eligibility must be confirmed with ABPN and the relevant program.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately describes the MGH/McLean programme page?

options.text: It offers only a conventional four-year adult psychiatry residency.
It describes a five- or six-year institutional Peds/Adult/Child Psychiatry route, plus separate adult-residency-then-CAP-fellowship and fast-track options.
It proves every trainee earns two ABPN certifications.
It is a directory category with no clinical training.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The institution’s page states the 5/6-year integrated route and also outlines other pathways. It does not prove each board certification or programme accreditation status.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has longstanding, cross-setting inattention and impairment, but school and family data differ. What is the best reasoning?

options.text: Use the difference as evidence that one informant is lying.
Clarify setting, developmental timeline, demands, and additional sources; treat ratings as evidence to synthesize, not a diagnosis alone.
Rule out ADHD because reports are not identical.
Diagnose autism from inconsistent ratings.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Cross-setting histories require interpretation of contextual differences and development; no single report or rating scale is dispositive.

practiceQuestions.stem: A young person has chronic irritability. Which feature most helps assess a bipolar-spectrum hypothesis?

options.text: Irritability by itself.
Distinct episodic change from baseline with associated energy/sleep and other syndromal features, impairment, collateral and alternative causes.
A single conflict with a caregiver.
Whether the family used the word “manic.”

practiceQuestions.rationale: Irritability is nonspecific. Longitudinal episodicity and the complete clinical context matter; do not treat it as pathognomonic.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with restrictive eating presents with syncope and concerning vital signs. Which principle is most important?

options.text: Manage as an outpatient psychiatric issue without medical review.
Urgently involve qualified medical care and assess instability; psychiatric-only management is insufficient.
Diagnose based on body size alone.
Use a psychotropic medication as a substitute for medical evaluation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Eating-disorder presentations can carry acute medical risk; medical stability and multidisciplinary evaluation take priority. This is a general educational principle, not a protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: When a freely viewable medication lecture provides a dose example, what is the correct self-study practice?

options.text: Apply the dose without checking age, indication or current labeling.
Treat the recording as dated educational material; verify current FDA label/guidelines, indication, contraindications, monitoring, and patient-specific supervision.
Assume all uses described are FDA-approved.
Convert the lecture into treatment instructions for an actual patient.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free viewing does not guarantee currency or applicability. Individual prescribing and monitoring require current primary sources and qualified clinicians.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about public clinical case reports and images is appropriate?

options.text: Free-to-view means unrestricted republication of case text and images.
Link and cite the source; check its licence/consent terms before reuse and never copy patient records or images into this course.
Anonymized photos can be reposted without permission.
Case reports can be treated as representative prevalence data.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Public access is not a reuse licence. Follow journal/author terms, respect privacy and consent, and avoid patient image/record copying; case reports do not establish population estimates.

title: Dermatology/Internal Medicine Residency
level: Clinical physician residency (combined Internal Medicine–Dermatology; independent self-study course, not residency)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Advanced health-professions/medical school level: anatomy, physiology, pathophysiology, microbiology, pharmacology and basic clinical epidemiology.
Learner should already have supervised clinical education; this self-study course is not appropriate as independent diagnostic or treatment training.
Required: source appraisal, basic statistics, medication reconciliation, and clinical safety awareness.
objectives: Integrate dermatologic morphology and time course with internal-medicine differential diagnosis and organ-system risk.
Map cutaneous findings to ABIM and ABD published content domains and identify limits of the evidence.
Build cautious, source-cited problem representations, differentials, test rationales and escalation plans for fictional educational cases.
Use current guideline summaries to describe management considerations without individual treatment advice.
Explain board certification and ACGME boundaries for combined medicine-dermatology training.

units.title: Clinical reasoning at the skin–system interface
objectives: Frame a problem representation from tempo, morphology, distribution, symptoms, exposures, medications, and organ-system clues.
Generate and prioritize dermatologic and systemic differentials without treating a morphology as a diagnosis.
boardDomains: ABD medical dermatology; ABIM clinical judgment
units.casePractice: Use an image-resource case link only; submit a one-page problem representation and ranked differential; no copied image.
units.assessment: Scored rubric: clinical reasoning and prioritization 40%; source/date accuracy 25%; uncertainty/safety boundaries 20%; clarity and equity 15%. Completion is formative, not a credential.

units.title: Eczematous, papulosquamous and inflammatory disease
objectives: Distinguish common eczematous, psoriasiform, lichenoid and scaly-rash patterns using history and morphology.
Choose when to reconsider a presumed diagnosis and when diagnostic testing/biopsy is warranted.
topics: Atopic/contact dermatitis, psoriasis, lichen planus, pityriasis rosea, erythroderma
units.casePractice: Compare a fictional scaly-rash differential and cite guideline-supported reasons to escalate.
units.assessment: Scored rubric: clinical reasoning and prioritization 40%; source/date accuracy 25%; uncertainty/safety boundaries 20%; clarity and equity 15%. Completion is formative, not a credential.

units.title: Infection, infestation and urgent rash patterns
objectives: Separate likely bacterial/fungal/viral/infestation categories and identify severe/systemic patterns requiring urgent assessment.
Use exposure, immune status and distribution to prioritize tests and safe escalation.
boardDomains: ABD medical dermatology; ABIM infectious disease
units.casePractice: Construct an urgency matrix, stating missing data and immediate escalation triggers.
units.assessment: Scored rubric: clinical reasoning and prioritization 40%; source/date accuracy 25%; uncertainty/safety boundaries 20%; clarity and equity 15%. Completion is formative, not a credential.

units.title: Drug eruptions and immune-mediated cutaneous toxicity
objectives: Build an exposure timeline and distinguish common exanthems from high-risk mucocutaneous/systemic reactions.
Recognize limits of causal certainty and communicate a safety-focused differential.

units.assessment: Scored rubric: clinical reasoning and prioritization 40%; source/date accuracy 25%; uncertainty/safety boundaries 20%; clarity and equity 15%. Completion is formative, not a credential.

units.title: Autoimmune connective tissue, vasculitic and blistering disease
objectives: Connect skin findings to targeted organ review and test interpretation rather than over-relying on a single antibody.
Identify kidney, lung, hematologic, neurologic and mucosal involvement that warrants cross-specialty coordination.
units.casePractice: Map skin/systemic clues and recommend a supervised workup plan with uncertainty labels.
units.assessment: Scored rubric: clinical reasoning and prioritization 40%; source/date accuracy 25%; uncertainty/safety boundaries 20%; clarity and equity 15%. Completion is formative, not a credential.

units.title: Skin clues to systemic disease and inpatient consult reasoning
objectives: Use dermatologic signs as prompts for—but not proof of—systemic disease.
Present concise consult questions, urgency and cross-specialty differential.
topics: Endocarditis/embolic clues, renal/hepatic manifestations, nutritional/metabolic clues, neutrophilic dermatoses, febrile rash, inpatient consult communication.

units.casePractice: Write a consult note problem representation and prioritized next-step questions.
units.assessment: Scored rubric: clinical reasoning and prioritization 40%; source/date accuracy 25%; uncertainty/safety boundaries 20%; clarity and equity 15%. Completion is formative, not a credential.

units.title: Internal medicine foundations: cardiovascular, renal and acid-base
objectives: Interpret common cardiology/nephrology concepts and connect medication/systemic disease effects to skin.
Use structured assessment for acute chest symptoms, rhythm, hemodynamics, AKI/electrolytes and acid-base cases.
topics: Cardiology, EKG concepts, arrhythmia, ACS, heart failure, hypertension, AKI, glomerular syndromes, electrolytes/acid-base.
units.casePractice: Solve 3 original cases with evidence citation and explicitly separate learning from treatment decisions.
units.assessment: Scored rubric: clinical reasoning and prioritization 40%; source/date accuracy 25%; uncertainty/safety boundaries 20%; clarity and equity 15%. Completion is formative, not a credential.

units.title: Rheumatology, allergy and immune-mediated disease
objectives: Interpret ANA and autoimmune testing in pretest-probability context; avoid diagnosis by isolated test.
Relate inflammatory disease manifestations to skin, kidney, lung and cardiovascular domains.
topics: Connective-tissue disease, spondyloarthropathies, immune testing, allergy/immunotherapy, anaphylaxis/urticaria, immunodeficiency.
units.casePractice: Make a differential-and-test map; state what a positive test does and does not establish.
units.assessment: Scored rubric: clinical reasoning and prioritization 40%; source/date accuracy 25%; uncertainty/safety boundaries 20%; clarity and equity 15%. Completion is formative, not a credential.

units.title: Cutaneous neoplasia and cancer-associated medicine
objectives: Recognize suspicious lesions and explain why biopsy adequacy, histology and stage govern subsequent decisions.

topics: Melanoma, keratinocyte cancers, precancers, staging concepts, systemic therapy toxicities, surveillance principles.
units.casePractice: Annotate an AAD guideline-based decision tree; no patient-level treatment recommendation.
units.assessment: Scored rubric: clinical reasoning and prioritization 40%; source/date accuracy 25%; uncertainty/safety boundaries 20%; clarity and equity 15%. Completion is formative, not a credential.

units.casePractice: Critique a fictional test-selection pathway for yield, harms and alternatives.
units.assessment: Scored rubric: clinical reasoning and prioritization 40%; source/date accuracy 25%; uncertainty/safety boundaries 20%; clarity and equity 15%. Completion is formative, not a credential.

topics: Psoriasis/AD comorbidity, cardiovascular/metabolic risk, skin cancer prevention, adherence, stigma, health equity, continuity.

units.assessment: Scored rubric: clinical reasoning and prioritization 40%; source/date accuracy 25%; uncertainty/safety boundaries 20%; clarity and equity 15%. Completion is formative, not a credential.

units.title: Board-style synthesis, uncertainty and safe handoffs
objectives: Use single-best-answer reasoning, prioritize immediate threats, and distinguish diagnosis from screening clue.

assignment.title: Integrated skin-system consult portfolio (fictional vignettes only)
deliverables: 12 short case reasoning briefs (one per unit); source citations and version dates

Two-minute verbal handoff script emphasizing uncertainty and red flags
assignment.passCriterion: Formative 80% target on original course quiz plus all safety/uncertainty rubric items satisfactory. Not validated, not official board scoring, and not predictive of exam success.

assessment.method: Low-stakes formative original single-best-answer questions; case-based synthesis; source-traceable rubric. No proprietary board questions.
assessment.limit: This course assessment is not psychometrically validated, has no proctoring or clinical performance observation, and cannot predict board success or license competence.
