topicGaps: Dermatology track: 19.454 observed hours against a 36-hour track floor; 16.546 hours remain. New verified recordings substantially deepen dermatopathology and skin-cancer coverage, but the residual cannot be filled by counted media found in this search. Future clip targets do not count as rendered or externally verified hours.

Combined two-track course: 59.804 unique verified free recording hours against the 72-hour combined target; 12.196 hours remain. The dermatology-specific deficit is binding even though the available Internal Medicine videos alone exceed 36 hours.

Internal Medicine: 40.351 verified hours are concentrated in the existing UofL cardiovascular, renal, rheumatology, and allergy/immunology series. The full IM blueprint remains uneven; pulmonary/critical care, broad infectious disease, endocrine, gastroenterology/hepatology, hematology/oncology, neurology, geriatrics, preventive care, and broad ambulatory synthesis lack adequate verified lecture coverage.

Dermatology: insufficient coverage remains for broad cutaneous infection/infestation beyond the current series, skin-of-color image-based pattern learning, pediatric dermatology, hair/nail, procedural/surgical and pharmacology domains, and supervised clinicopathologic case conference. Existing accessible videos provide selected pattern instruction only; they do not replace image licensing, clinical observation, or current specialty references.

A public lupus webinar and several listed pathology videos were inspected as sources but not added when an exact usable duration and reliably accessible full player could not both be established. Duration-unknown or uncertain-access entries remain uncounted.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.boardStatus: Two separate specialty boards/examination pathways: ABIM Internal Medicine and ABD Dermatology (ABD CORE exams followed by APPLIED examination). officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Exact institutional label preserved from the discovery packet. medical.programmeSourceScope: Verified from Harvard Combined Dermatology, BWH/MGB and boards’ public webpages. 5 years/60 months, 30 months per specialty, distributed clinical experience. Public description identifies rotations at BWH and dermatology at BWH, MGH, BIDMC, Boston Children’s, Lahey and Boston VA. It does not provide a complete didactic video set, all rotations’ dates, or patient volume. Institution-wide directory listing is a discovery signal, not accreditation evidence. ACGME identifies Dermatology–Internal Medicine as a combined-program category; ABIM policy now requires combined ACGME accreditation (since 2025). Individual current programme accreditation record not independently inspected; verify directly in ACGME ADS before using accreditation claims.
sourceCaveats: Clinical guidelines change; AAD 2025 adult atopic dermatitis update and published guideline summary were checked on 2026-10-07. Check current version before application.
The source program’s 2025–26 match dates and past match-number discrepancies were not included as current eligibility facts.
Harvard/BWH wording is descriptive of program candidates/residents; it is not an independent confirmation of present ACGME accreditation status or any individual’s eligibility.

The ACGME 2026 Combined Programs page lists Dermatology–Internal Medicine as a combined category; ABIM’s new combined-accreditation requirement applies from 2025. ADS-level status for the institution was not independently validated.

Video hours are public playlist metadata durations. A video’s listing/free access can change, and metadata was not a watch-through validation. No playlist repeats, duplicates, snippets, planned clips, unknown-duration entries, or non-video readings are counted. Duplicates identified by video ID counted once.

Image pages are linked only; free-to-view does not automatically grant republication rights. DermNet case-level anonymization/consent was not validated; no clinical image/patient record was copied. MedPix case-level terms were unavailable in the stateless review.

Human clinical review has NOT been performed. The course is independent, unaffiliated self-study and does not grant accredited training, license, eligibility, procedural competence, certificate, or guaranteed board success.

Internal Medicine: 40.351 verified hours are concentrated in the existing UofL cardiovascular, renal, rheumatology, and allergy/immunology series. The full IM blueprint remains uneven; pulmonary/critical care, broad infectious disease, endocrine, gastroenterology/hepatology, hematology/oncology, neurology, geriatrics, preventive care, and broad ambulatory synthesis lack adequate verified lecture coverage.

Dermatology: insufficient coverage remains for broad cutaneous infection/infestation beyond the current series, skin-of-color image-based pattern learning, pediatric dermatology, hair/nail, procedural/surgical and pharmacology domains, and supervised clinicopathologic case conference. Existing accessible videos provide selected pattern instruction only; they do not replace image licensing, clinical observation, or current specialty references.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 42-year-old has a new widespread erythematous eruption after beginning a medication. Which first step best supports safe reasoning?

options.text: Establish chronology, complete medication/exposure list and assess mucosal/systemic red flags
Label it a benign exanthem from morphology alone
Stop every chronic medication without review
Order ANA as a universal rash screen

practiceQuestions.rationale: A medication timeline and severity/red-flag assessment improve causal reasoning and identify emergencies; no single morphology or screening test establishes cause.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABD medical dermatology; ABIM clinical judgment

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with suspected atopic dermatitis has persistent disease despite an apparently optimized regimen. What is the best next reasoning step?

options.text: Reassess diagnosis and consider mimics/coexisting disease; targeted testing may be appropriate
Escalate systemic steroids as routine long-term treatment
Assume allergy testing is mandatory for all patients
Dismiss symptoms as nonadherence

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAD describes diagnostic reassessment in treatment-resistant presumed adult AD and against systemic corticosteroids as routine treatment; testing is scenario-specific.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about psoriasis evaluation is most accurate?

options.text: PASI is recommended as a routine clinical practice tool
Psoriasis is multisystem; assess severity, symptoms/QoL and relevant comorbidities
Skin extent alone fully captures impact
Systemic steroids are the standard maintenance therapy

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAD describes psoriasis as multisystem, recommends clinical severity measures such as BSA/PGA and patient impact, and notes PASI is recommended for trials rather than routine clinical practice.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with fever and a new rash has oral erosions and skin pain. Which approach is safest?

options.text: Urgent assessment for severe cutaneous adverse reaction/systemic illness; do not delay escalation for a routine outpatient workup
Treat as uncomplicated eczema without further history
Use a photo alone to decide the diagnosis
Wait for rash to evolve before checking vital signs

practiceQuestions.rationale: Mucosal involvement, skin pain and fever are red flags requiring urgent in-person evaluation; this is a triage principle, not a definitive diagnosis.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABD medical dermatology; ABIM infectious disease

practiceQuestions.stem: An isolated positive ANA is found in a patient with nonspecific fatigue but no other findings. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: It establishes SLE
It must be interpreted with history, exam, pretest probability and other evidence
It proves active nephritis
It automatically warrants immunosuppression

practiceQuestions.rationale: ANA is one component of a broader clinical evaluation; lupus has no single definitive test and similar symptoms occur in other diseases.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with chronic inflammatory skin disease reports swollen joints and prolonged morning stiffness. What is the most appropriate educational reasoning?

options.text: Consider associated inflammatory arthritis and coordinate further assessment rather than assuming skin-only disease
Conclude the skin disease caused irreversible joint damage
Ignore the symptom if the rash is mild
Use PASI to diagnose arthritis

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAD recognizes psoriatic arthritis among important comorbidities and emphasizes primary-care attention; skin assessment alone cannot diagnose joint disease.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pigmented lesion is clinically suspicious. Which principle is consistent with AAD melanoma guidance?

options.text: Adequate histopathologic diagnosis informs management; staging and sentinel node decisions are risk/stage dependent
A smartphone image alone substitutes for histology
All melanomas require the same surveillance imaging
Nonsurgical treatment is preferred whenever convenient

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAD highlights biopsy methods that preserve diagnostic histopathology; staging and sentinel node biopsy apply in appropriate cases, with follow-up based on stage and risk.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has rash, edema, hypertension and abnormal urinalysis. What is the best integrated approach?

options.text: Treat the rash as the sole disease and ignore renal signals
Prioritize evaluation of possible systemic/renal involvement with appropriate supervised cross-specialty workup
Diagnose lupus nephritis from rash alone
Assume edema is a medication effect without review

practiceQuestions.rationale: Lupus and other systemic disorders may involve skin and kidneys; findings require clinical evaluation, differential diagnosis and targeted tests rather than certainty from skin clues.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABD medical dermatology; ABIM multisystem clinical reasoning

options.text: Link to the source and respect its image-specific terms; do not copy/rehost by default
Download and crop away the watermark for slides
Assume every free-to-view image is public domain
Upload images to train an AI classifier

practiceQuestions.rationale: DermNet says watermarked images have noncommercial/no-derivatives and attribution conditions; no default permission for commercial or AI reuse. Link-only is the safe default.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABD basic science/medical dermatology; ABIM diagnostic reasoning

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the ABIM/ABD status of the combined pathway?

options.text: It is one combined examination issued by the residency
Program pages describe eligibility for separate internal medicine and dermatology boards after qualifying accredited training; self-study does not create eligibility
Course completion grants both certifications
No board examinations exist

practiceQuestions.rationale: The institutions name both board exams; ABIM combined requirements specify an integrated 60-month course and ACGME combined accreditation requirement beginning 2025. Certification remains board-controlled.

title: Global Health Equity Residency
level: Combined clinical physician residency pathway in Internal Medicine and Global Health Equity with MPH coursework (not a standalone board-certified specialty or research-only appointment)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Advanced-level learners with prior medical-school internal-medicine foundations; intended for residents, fellows, physicians and public-health learners who can interpret basic clinical and epidemiologic concepts.
Familiarity with adult history/examination, common syndromes, basic statistics, study designs and research ethics is assumed.
Learners without clinical training may use the equity, policy and methods units but should not act on clinical material.
objectives: Integrate clinical reasoning with structural and social determinants while avoiding diagnostic stereotyping.
Interpret public-health and clinical evidence with uncertainty, denominator awareness and test limitations.
Apply current authoritative infectious-disease resources as context-specific references rather than portable prescriptions.
Design a reciprocal, ethical and locally governed global-health or domestic equity programme.
Use health services, financing, implementation, evaluation and policy frameworks to address a defined disparity.
Recognize that ABIM internal medicine certification depends on actual accredited training, licensure, competence and examination; this course grants none of these.

units.title: Global health equity: concepts, history, power and structural drivers
objectives: Distinguish health equity from equality and describe avoidable, unjust health gaps.
Build a multilevel causal map from structural conditions to access, exposure, disease and outcomes without reducing inequity to individual behavior.
Critique how colonial history, resource distribution, racism, gender and local power shape programme design.
topics: Global health actors and postcolonial critique
boardDomains: ABIM cross-cutting health equity; epidemiology/risk assessment; general internal medicine
units.casePractice: Fictional clinic referral scenario: map transport, cost, language and policy barriers separately from biological differential; do not assume a single determinant explains an outcome.
units.assessment: Submit a one-page causal diagram and 300-word interpretation distinguishing patient-level association from upstream causes.

units.title: Internal medicine reasoning across settings
objectives: Use problem representation and illness scripts for common adult presentations in unfamiliar epidemiologic contexts.
Select initial tests using pretest probability, urgency, test performance, harms and follow-up feasibility.
Identify uncertainty and escalate time-critical syndromes through local clinical pathways.
topics: ABIM task domains: diagnosis/testing, care decisions, prognosis, pathophysiology
Fever, dyspnea, anemia and chronic disease as syndromic entry points
Context-sensitive differential and diagnostic safety nets
boardDomains: ABIM Internal Medicine: broad clinical categories; diagnosis/testing and treatment/care decisions
units.casePractice: Fictional returning traveller with fever: prioritize dangerous and treatable causes; articulate what information would change the differential; no definitive diagnosis is supplied.
units.assessment: Write a problem representation, ranked differential with explicit uncertainty and staged testing plan; grading rewards reasoning, not an asserted final diagnosis.

units.title: High-burden infections: HIV, tuberculosis, malaria and emerging threats
objectives: Relate disease burden and transmission to clinical presentation, prevention and health-system access.
Interpret diagnostic pathways and population-level recommendations with attention to current local/national guidance.
Discuss comorbidity, drug resistance, continuity and equity in infectious-disease programmes.
topics: HIV clinical management and treatment cascade
TB diagnosis, treatment, infection prevention and TB/HIV
Malaria as urgent febrile illness; global guidance versus U.S. imported-case guidance
boardDomains: ABIM Infectious Disease (9% of initial certification blueprint, approximate); pulmonary; hematology; prevention; epidemiology
units.casePractice: Use a public outbreak teaching case or a fictional TB/HIV clinic scenario; do not copy patient data or infer local prevalence from one case.
units.assessment: Compare two official guideline contexts and identify one clinical decision, one equity barrier and one data limitation.

units.title: Maternal, child and adolescent health equity
objectives: Identify life-course, reproductive, neonatal and adolescent dimensions in adult-medicine global health work.
Interpret maternal/child health disparities in their demographic, economic and health-service context.
Design a respectful referral and continuity map that preserves patient agency and avoids stereotyping.
boardDomains: ABIM Obstetrics/Gynecology (3%); Pediatrics not a core ABIM specialty domain but relevant cross-cutting prevention and infectious disease
units.casePractice: Fictional maternal-health referral case with language and transport barriers; learners identify what is known, missing and appropriate to ask, not make a real-patient recommendation.
units.assessment: Create a one-page pathway map, including consent, referral ownership and measures of reach and outcome.

units.title: Population health, epidemiology and clinical evidence
objectives: Interpret absolute and relative risks, rates, confounding, selection bias and effect modification.
Use burden-of-disease and surveillance data while checking denominators, completeness and representativeness.
Translate a population signal into a cautious clinical or service-delivery question.
boardDomains: ABIM Clinical Epidemiology; risk assessment/prognosis/epidemiology; diagnosis/testing
units.casePractice: CDC applied-epidemiology teaching cases based on real investigations (link only; see rights conditions in Cases).
units.assessment: Calculate and interpret a 2x2 table from synthetic data, identify a bias pathway, and propose a safe next data step.

units.title: Primary care, health systems, continuity and universal coverage
objectives: Compare health-system organization and service models without treating one setting as a universal template.
Analyze referral, supply, workforce and continuity constraints that shape treatment feasibility.
Propose a locally co-designed service improvement with accountability and feedback.
topics: Primary health care and universal health coverage
Community health workers, referral networks and task-sharing
boardDomains: ABIM prevention, patient safety, care decisions, cross-cutting health equity
units.casePractice: Trace a fictional chronic-disease referral through primary care, laboratory and specialty services; mark failure points and local decision-makers.
units.assessment: Submit a service blueprint with patient journey, bottleneck, partner roles and balancing measure.

units.title: Financing, economics and stewardship
objectives: Explain how financing, procurement and affordability influence access and clinical decisions.
Distinguish cost-effectiveness, budget impact, financial protection and cost minimization.
Make a transparent, equity-aware resource-allocation argument using stated assumptions.
topics: Value for money and opportunity cost
boardDomains: ABIM risk assessment/prognosis, prevention and treatment/care decisions; global health programme competence (not a separate board domain)
units.casePractice: Synthetic district-budget exercise; all prices and outcome values supplied as invented teaching data, not factual country estimates.
units.assessment: Two-page policy memo with assumptions, comparator, equity impact, opportunity cost and sensitivity analysis.

units.title: Humanitarian health, conflict, migration and health security
objectives: Assess how displacement, conflict, access restrictions and disrupted services affect clinical risk and continuity.
Apply ethical triage and protection principles without stereotyping displaced groups.
Plan safe coordination, referral and information-sharing at a systems level.
boardDomains: ABIM infectious disease, prevention, ethics, patient safety and acute-care reasoning
units.casePractice: Use a published teaching case at source; no actual patient records, images or real operational coordinates are imported.
units.assessment: Draft a short tabletop response identifying clinical priorities, rights, referral handoffs, uncertainty and safety triggers.

units.title: Clinical, public-health and research ethics; reciprocal partnership
objectives: Apply consent, privacy, fair selection, benefit sharing and community engagement to research and care.
Identify unequal power and extractive patterns; formulate reciprocal and accountable partnership terms.
Distinguish clinical care, public-health surveillance, quality improvement and human-subject research questions.
topics: Research ethics and IRB/ethics committee review
boardDomains: ABIM Ethics and health-equity cross-cutting content
units.casePractice: Analyze a fictional partnership proposal with community representatives as decision-makers; no identifiable examples or real participants.
units.assessment: Complete an ethics-and-partnership checklist; rubric prioritizes local governance, fair benefit and clear limits on data use.

units.title: Global health research methods and implementation science
objectives: Frame an answerable research or implementation question with appropriate outcomes and design.
Distinguish efficacy, effectiveness, implementation outcomes and sustainability.
Describe transparent data governance, equity stratification and responsible dissemination.
topics: Mixed methods, pragmatic measurement and uncertainty
boardDomains: ABIM clinical epidemiology, risk/prognosis and evidence-informed care
units.casePractice: Critique a linked public case study/report for sampling, measurement, transferability and community voice.
units.assessment: Write a 1-page protocol synopsis with question, design, measures, partners, ethics and limitations.

units.title: Policy, advocacy, leadership and programme evaluation
objectives: Map stakeholders and decision authority before proposing policy or programme changes.
Build a logic model with outputs, outcomes, unintended effects and accountability.
Communicate evidence to technical and community audiences without overclaiming causal certainty.
boardDomains: ABIM prevention, clinical epidemiology, health equity and risk/benefit reasoning
units.casePractice: Analyze a public country/programme case selected from WHO/TEPHINET; adapt only with local partner input.
units.assessment: Present a 5-minute stakeholder brief plus one-page monitoring framework; include a counterargument and feedback loop.

units.title: Planetary health, environment, nutrition and cross-sectoral action
objectives: Connect environmental exposures, climate and food systems to clinical and population-health risks.
Describe co-benefits and trade-offs of cross-sectoral interventions.
Propose proportionate, measurable actions while distinguishing evidence from advocacy claims.
boardDomains: ABIM preventive medicine, pulmonary disease, endocrinology/diabetes, epidemiology and health equity
units.casePractice: Use a fictional community respiratory/nutrition scenario; build a causal map and avoid attributing a single clinical outcome to climate exposure.
units.assessment: Submit a cross-sector intervention logic model with clinical relevance, distributional impacts and evaluation plan.

assignment.title: Equity-focused clinical-service improvement dossier
deliverables: A two-page problem statement and causal map separating clinical mechanisms from structural/service determinants.
A short evidence table with population, denominator, design, key uncertainty and source date.
A co-design and governance plan that identifies local decision-makers, consent/privacy protections and reciprocal benefit.
A feasible service/intervention logic model with clinical outcome, access/reach measure, equity stratifier, balancing measure and budget assumption.
A five-minute oral stakeholder briefing plus reflective paragraph naming one uncertainty and one potential harm.

rubric.standard: Clear problem representation, differential, urgent risks, uncertainty and jurisdiction-aware current guidance.
Distinguishes individual, service and structural pathways; avoids essentialism and overclaiming.
Appropriate denominator/design, transparent assumptions, limitations and current source citations.
Local governance, reciprocity, consent/privacy, feasible roles and accountability.
Measurable feasible plan, unintended effects, budget logic and clear audience-appropriate communication.

assignment.grading: Score 0–4 on each criterion and multiply by weight. A course-completion target of 80/100 is a self-study threshold only, not validated competence or a board predictor.

assessment.rubric: Pass threshold is a local learning target only (80% recommended on original practice items and at least 80/100 dossier score); not a validated exam predictor or certification. Revisit missed questions against source guidance.

studyHours.basis: Transparent self-study plan: 46.1 observed public-video hours; 30 hours open readings; 25 hours case assignments and dossier; 12 hours original questions/review; 6.9 hours reflection and synthesis. Non-video components are learner-time planning estimates, not measured instructional contact hours. Video count is separately documented in ledger.

mapping.name: Global Health Equity Residency
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Current MGB training page describes the Doris and Howard Hiatt Residency in Global Health Equity and Internal Medicine as a 48-month multidisciplinary physician residency: 33 months clinical IM including continuity clinic and 11 months field work, research and coursework, with MPH study through Harvard Chan and a statement that it leads to ABIM IM eligibility. It names potential field sites and says options vary; no complete rotation matrix or hours ledger is published.

mapping.institution: Brigham and Women’s Hospital
mapping.name: Doris and Howard Hiatt Residency in Global Health Equity and Internal Medicine
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: BWH programme page gives the same pathway name, BWH IM PGY-1 applicant route, 48-month curriculum, 33 clinical and 11 field/research/coursework months, public-health graduate coursework and global-health seminars. It describes eligibility for ABIM certification contingent on the real programme, not this independent course.

medical.trackType: Combined clinical physician residency pathway in Internal Medicine and Global Health Equity with MPH coursework (not a standalone board-certified specialty or research-only appointment)
boardNames: American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) — Internal Medicine Certification Examination
medical.boardStatus: The institutional pathway is publicly described as leading toward ABIM Internal Medicine certification eligibility; Global Health Equity itself is not a separate ABMS/ABIM specialty certificate or examination. A distinct ABIM Internal Medicine Certification Examination exists. This course is not an accredited residency and grants no board eligibility.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: MGB/BWH programme pages state this four-year pathway leads to ABIM eligibility, subject to the official accredited clinical training, licensure, competence and board policies. ABIM’s standard pathway specifies 36 months of accredited U.S./Canadian GME, including at least 30 clinical months, plus other requirements and examination. BWH publicly describes the expanded pathway as 48 months with 33 clinical months and 11 months of field work/research/coursework; public materials do not expose the full rotation-by-rotation credit table. The programme statement and ABIM rules should be confirmed with the programme and ABIM; do not infer individual eligibility from the public summary.

officialProgrammes.institution: Mass General Brigham
officialProgrammes.name: Global Health Equity Residency
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Current MGB training page describes the Doris and Howard Hiatt Residency in Global Health Equity and Internal Medicine as a 48-month multidisciplinary physician residency: 33 months clinical IM including continuity clinic and 11 months field work, research and coursework, with MPH study through Harvard Chan and a statement that it leads to ABIM IM eligibility. It names potential field sites and says options vary; no complete rotation matrix or hours ledger is published.

officialProgrammes.institution: Brigham and Women’s Hospital
officialProgrammes.name: Doris and Howard Hiatt Residency in Global Health Equity and Internal Medicine
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: BWH programme page gives the same pathway name, BWH IM PGY-1 applicant route, 48-month curriculum, 33 clinical and 11 field/research/coursework months, public-health graduate coursework and global-health seminars. It describes eligibility for ABIM certification contingent on the real programme, not this independent course.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The packet’s MGB directory item is not merely a generic directory category: its linked official programme page identifies a named BWH Global Health Equity/Internal Medicine combined physician residency pathway. This is a special track within the BWH Internal Medicine residency plus MPH/public-health training and field/research work, rather than a separate standalone ABIM specialty. The assigned discovery item is preserved as one item; Johns Hopkins Global Health Pathway is a contextual comparator only, not another institutional variant. The public page describes prospective international/domestic partner sites; it does not prove every trainee rotates at every site or publish a guaranteed rotation schedule. The programme includes longitudinal research, but is not a research-only postdoctoral job.
sourceCaveats: Current MGB page states 33 months of clinical training plus 11 months field work/research/coursework. The publicly listed summary does not supply the detailed schedule needed to independently reconcile the program’s accreditation/ABIM pathway with the board’s standard 36-month/30-clinical-month requirements. Confirm with BWH and ABIM.

The MGB/BWH pages report training plans and applicant criteria as current but cohort schedules and project sites can change. A list of planned sites is not proof of personal rotations, eligibility, outcomes or guaranteed placement.

ABIM blueprint domains and percentages represent an exam blueprint, not this residency’s curriculum or a guarantee of item frequency. Course maps domains but does not comprehensively teach every ABIM category.

Global video runtime totals rely on playlist public metadata. Anonymous oEmbed confirmed 74 selected titles/authors. Automated direct player extraction returned anti-bot errors, which were not bypassed; free playability can change and should be rechecked.
Human clinical review has not been performed. WHO/CDC guidance may update; verify current recommendations and local protocols before clinical use.
Free-to-view does not grant republication, download, embedding or patient-image reuse rights. Link to resources, respect source licenses and request permission where needed.

No human cases, patient charts, diagnostic images, actual case volume, eligibility determination, licensure, independent procedure competence, board passing predictor, affiliation or accredited training is provided.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult returns from a malaria-endemic region with fever and rigors. Initial clinical information is incomplete. Which next-step principle is safest?

options.text: Treat as uncomplicated viral illness unless a rash appears.
Promptly evaluate for malaria and other time-critical causes using the current local diagnostic pathway; do not let a social barrier substitute for the clinical differential.
Wait for a single outpatient follow-up test next week.
Infer malaria from travel history alone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Malaria can progress rapidly; CDC guidance stresses urgent diagnosis and immediate treatment. Exposure raises pretest probability but is not diagnostic; assess other causes and use current local guidance. This question provides no treatment instruction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician reviewing a TB-clinic programme observes fewer completed visits among people with long travel times. Which interpretation best separates upstream determinants from individual blame?

options.text: Patients are less motivated.
Travel burden may mediate access and continuity; measure it with service design and patient input before assigning causation.
The finding proves clinic quality is poor.
The association establishes that travel causes disease progression.

practiceQuestions.rationale: WHO locates health determinants in living conditions and access to resources; an observed association does not establish a causal effect. Measure the pathway and solicit affected communities’ interpretation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A report compares TB treatment completion before and after a programme launch, with no comparison group and changes in case mix. What is the main limitation?

options.text: The before-after difference alone cannot isolate programme effect from secular trends or case-mix changes.
A before-after design always proves the intervention works.
No denominator is needed if totals are large.
Any observed improvement proves equity increased.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A simple before-after contrast is vulnerable to confounding, time trends and changed population composition; equity effects need defined subgroup denominators and a credible design.

practiceQuestions.stem: A collaborator proposes publishing identifiable facility-level data from a small community without local review because no names are included. What should the team do first?

options.text: Publish immediately because aggregate data are never sensitive.
Assess re-identification risk, community governance, consent/ethics obligations and local review before dissemination.
Remove only one variable and proceed.
Ask the international sponsor to decide alone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: WHO research ethics protects dignity, rights and welfare; small-cell or contextual data may identify groups even without names. Seek appropriate ethics review and community governance.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public-health intervention shows the same average coverage across two areas but has much lower reach among a marginalized subgroup. What is the best next analytic step?

options.text: Report only the average.
Disaggregate responsibly, investigate the access pathway with affected partners and assess subgroup outcomes and privacy risk.
Conclude the intervention is equitable because overall coverage is equal.
Use ethnicity as a biological cause.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Health equity requires attention to unfair avoidable gaps and how social conditions shape access. Stratify with safeguards and interpret social identifiers as context, not biological explanation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional district must choose between a higher-cost service that benefits few people and a less costly service that may broaden access. Which appraisal is most defensible?

options.text: Choose the least costly option without checking outcomes.
State comparator, perspective, budget impact, opportunity cost and distributional effects, then test assumptions.
Use cost-effectiveness ratio alone as a final ethical rule.
Assume more expensive means more effective.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Stewardship decisions require transparent assumptions and assessment of value, budget impact and equity; economic indicators do not by themselves settle distributive ethics.

practiceQuestions.stem: A community health programme uses a new screening test. The team only reports sensitivity. Which additional information best supports implementation planning?

options.text: Specificity, prevalence/pretest context, referral capacity, harms, follow-up and who may be missed.
The manufacturer’s marketing headline.
Only the total number of tests distributed.
A single anecdote from a pilot site.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Test performance and downstream consequences depend on prevalence, confirmation, service capacity and selection. ABIM assesses test ordering and interpretation together with treatment and risk tasks.

practiceQuestions.stem: A resident designs a field rotation at a new partner site with limited prior collaboration. What is the best initial approach?

options.text: Arrive with a fixed intervention and collect data immediately.
Map partners and decision authority, agree reciprocal goals and supervision, and establish local governance before clinical or research activity.
Treat a short elective as proof of local competence.
Use the partner site’s patient records in teaching slides.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The BWH pathway and Hopkins pathway describe mentorship, partner sites, scholarship and ethics; none authorizes independent practice. Reciprocity, local supervision and governance precede activity.

practiceQuestions.stem: A district reports rising malaria cases after enhanced testing was introduced. Which inference is most cautious?

options.text: Transmission definitely worsened.
Improved case detection could contribute; examine testing volume, positivity, case definitions, access and independent transmission indicators.
Testing has no effect on reported case counts.
The data prove the test is inaccurate.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Surveillance counts reflect both disease and detection processes. Interpret denominator, ascertainment, test properties and time trends before inferring transmission.

practiceQuestions.stem: A project finds that a digitally delivered follow-up model improves average attendance, but patients without reliable connectivity are excluded. Which evaluation response is strongest?

options.text: Declare success from the average alone.
Measure reach, outcomes and harms by connectivity/access, invite community feedback, and adapt delivery with an equity-oriented comparison.
Require every patient to use the app.
Exclude non-users from all future evaluation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Average outcomes can hide exclusion. CUGH competency guidance supports equity-focused design and evaluation; assess unintended effects and accessibility.

title: DAP StARR Residency Program — independent aging-research and clinical-reasoning curriculum
level: Research pathway supplement embedded in clinical physician residencies (not a distinct residency specialty)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.audience: Advanced self-study for residents/physicians, physician-scientists, clinical researchers and senior health-professions learners. Clinical specialty learning presumes prior medical education; no lay learner should use this for diagnosis or care.
requiredBackground: Basic human biology and clinical epidemiology
Research ethics and critical appraisal fundamentals
recommendedPreparation: Read the MGH DAP StARR official overview and NIH IPPCR course description.
Choose one public, non-identifiable research question about ADRD, frailty or multimorbidity.
Use only public aggregate or properly authorized de-identified data; no identifiable/patient records.
prerequisites.clinicalBoundary: Independent education only; no patient-care or procedure instruction, supervision, competency sign-off, licensure, institutional affiliation, accredited training or board eligibility.

objectives: Describe the DAP StARR pathway without confusing it with a separate residency, specialty, combined programme or board exam.
Construct clinically important, measurable and ethical aging-research questions.
Select and critique observational, diagnostic, experimental and implementation-study designs.
Interpret bias, uncertainty, missingness, clinical outcome validity and generalizability.
Design a responsible protocol with human-subjects safeguards, reproducibility, data governance, equity and dissemination.
Map research themes to the relevant ABIM/ABPN parent-board domains without claiming equivalence to a board examination or clinical training.

units.title: DAP StARR: research-in-residency, aging science and question formation
objectives: Explain DAP StARR as a mentored research pathway within existing IM/Neurology residencies, not a standalone specialty.
Translate ADRD, frailty or multimorbidity uncertainty into an answerable question.
Distinguish basic, translational, clinical and implementation research.
topics: R38/StARR purpose; aging-research ecosystem; researchable clinical uncertainty; PICO/PECO; equipoise; mentor and team roles.
boardDomains: ABPN: Normal structure/process across life cycle; behavioral neurology (context only)
units.casePractice: Create a one-page PICO/PECO question on one aging-related uncertainty and identify whether it is descriptive, causal, diagnostic or implementation research.

assessment.minimumStandard: At least 3 of 4 criteria demonstrated; faculty/clinical review is not performed by this self-study course.

units.title: Clinical phenotyping: cognition, frailty, function and multimorbidity
objectives: Differentiate screening, syndrome description and etiologic diagnosis.
Specify reproducible cognitive, functional and frailty constructs and time anchors.
Anticipate language, sensory, educational, cultural and informant effects.
topics: Cognition/function/frailty operational definitions; informant data; comorbidity and medication confounding; longitudinal phenotype; ascertainment validity.
boardDomains: ABPN: Behavioral neurology and neurocognitive disorders; clinical aspects
units.casePractice: Define an outcome and eligibility criteria for a fictional older-adult cohort; explain why a positive screen is not a disease diagnosis.

assessment.minimumStandard: At least 3 of 4 criteria demonstrated; faculty/clinical review is not performed by this self-study course.

units.title: Evidence synthesis, biological plausibility and research gap
objectives: Build a reproducible search and evidence table.
Assess selection, measurement and publication bias in aging research.
Separate biologic mechanism, association and clinical prediction.
topics: Question refinement; evidence hierarchy; systematic search; bias; certainty; replication; evidence gaps.
units.casePractice: Appraise two public studies using a structured extraction grid; separate design, population, outcomes, confounders and limitations.

assessment.minimumStandard: At least 3 of 4 criteria demonstrated; faculty/clinical review is not performed by this self-study course.

units.title: Study design and causal inference in aging cohorts
objectives: Choose an observational design or randomized trial for a specific estimand.
Explain confounding, selection, immortal-time and reverse-causality risks.
State what randomization does and does not identify.
topics: Cohort/case-control/cross-sectional/trial; target population; estimand; DAGs; time zero; competing risks; pragmatic trials.
boardDomains: ABIM: Clinical epidemiology; diagnosis/testing and risk/prognosis tasks
units.casePractice: Draft a protocol synopsis and DAG; grade it for question/design alignment, time zero and causal assumptions.

assessment.minimumStandard: At least 3 of 4 criteria demonstrated; faculty/clinical review is not performed by this self-study course.

units.title: Biostatistics, missingness and longitudinal outcomes
objectives: Interpret effect estimates and uncertainty rather than p-values alone.
Distinguish clinical importance from statistical significance.
Plan handling for missingness, repeated observations, competing risks and multiplicity.
topics: Descriptive/inferential statistics; confidence intervals; regression; sample size principles; missing data; survival/recurrent events; sensitivity analyses.
boardDomains: ABPN: Neuroepidemiology; diagnostic procedures; practice-based learning
units.casePractice: Interpret a hypothetical longitudinal table; recommend a prespecified missing-data sensitivity analysis and identify unsupported inference.

assessment.minimumStandard: At least 3 of 4 criteria demonstrated; faculty/clinical review is not performed by this self-study course.

units.title: Bioinformatics, biomarkers and reproducibility
objectives: Distinguish discovery from validation and clinical utility.
Describe batch, selection, leakage and multiplicity risks in high-dimensional aging datasets.
Specify a reproducible analysis plan and auditable workflow.
topics: Omics/data provenance; phenotype harmonization; batch effects; train/test leakage; external validation; analytical vs clinical validity; reproducibility.
units.casePractice: Review a fictional biomarker model card; identify leakage, validation and intended-use gaps.

assessment.minimumStandard: At least 3 of 4 criteria demonstrated; faculty/clinical review is not performed by this self-study course.

units.title: Human-subject protections, RCR, dementia consent and safety
objectives: Apply respect, beneficence and justice to older-adult research.
Identify consent-capacity assessment, surrogate involvement and participant assent/ongoing preference needs.
Explain IRB, adverse-event and independent safety-monitoring roles.
topics: RCR; consent and decision-making capacity; surrogate consent; assent; privacy; vulnerable populations; DSM/DSMB; unanticipated problems; conflicts of interest.
units.casePractice: Conduct a consent-risk tabletop for a fictional study without assuming age or cognitive diagnosis alone eliminates capacity.

assessment.minimumStandard: At least 3 of 4 criteria demonstrated; faculty/clinical review is not performed by this self-study course.

units.title: Trial design, measurement and translational endpoints
objectives: Map mechanism-to-endpoint assumptions.
Assess diagnostic test accuracy and clinical utility separately.
Describe protocol safety, monitoring and treatment-version control.
topics: Endpoints; surrogate validity; biomarker qualification; diagnostic accuracy; eligibility; outcome adjudication; harms; protocol versioning.
boardDomains: ABPN: diagnostic procedures; treatment/management; clinical aspects
units.casePractice: Critique an openly posted trial registry record for endpoint, population, comparator, recruitment, dates and public status; no efficacy conclusion from registry alone.

assessment.minimumStandard: At least 3 of 4 criteria demonstrated; faculty/clinical review is not performed by this self-study course.

units.title: Implementation science, health equity and inclusive recruitment
objectives: Select an implementation outcome and explain how it differs from clinical efficacy.
Audit representativeness, accessibility and differential measurement.
Plan community partnership and accessible communication without tokenization.
topics: Reach/adoption/fidelity/sustainability; health disparities; language access; structural barriers; recruitment/retention; transportability.
boardDomains: ABPN: Interpersonal/communication; systems-based practice; practice-based learning
units.casePractice: Perform a recruitment/transportability audit on a fictional ADRD study with prespecified subgroup data and engagement safeguards.

assessment.minimumStandard: At least 3 of 4 criteria demonstrated; faculty/clinical review is not performed by this self-study course.

units.title: Data governance, sharing, privacy and open science
objectives: Create a proportionate data-management plan.
Distinguish de-identification from anonymity and document residual re-identification risk.
Balance reproducibility and sharing with consent, HIPAA, tribal/community and institutional restrictions.
topics: Data dictionaries; access controls; retention; secure analysis; de-identification; NIH DMS; code/version control; FAIR/open science limits.
units.casePractice: Write a data-flow diagram and sharing statement for a fictional multicenter clinical cohort; no real patient data.

assessment.minimumStandard: At least 3 of 4 criteria demonstrated; faculty/clinical review is not performed by this self-study course.

units.title: Protocol, grants, scientific communication and peer review
objectives: Write aims, significance, approach, milestones and risks coherently.
Match method and sample size justification to a prespecified question.
Present limitations and negative results transparently.
topics: Specific aims; protocol; grant logic; feasibility; milestones; manuscript/abstract; peer review; figure integrity; stakeholder communication.
units.casePractice: Submit a three-aim, two-page protocol/grant synopsis and a 250-word plain-language abstract, using rubric below.

assessment.minimumStandard: At least 3 of 4 criteria demonstrated; faculty/clinical review is not performed by this self-study course.

units.title: Career development, mentorship, team science and translation
objectives: Construct an individual development plan and mentor compact.
Define roles, authorship, conflict resolution and clinical-skills continuity.
Explain translation boundaries between self-study, residency competence and independent practice.
topics: Mentoring; team science; authorship; research career development; protected time; translational pathways; clinical skill maintenance; dissemination.
units.casePractice: Prepare a one-year fictional IDP with research milestones, clinical continuity, mentoring cadence, dissemination and a contingency plan.

assessment.minimumStandard: At least 3 of 4 criteria demonstrated; faculty/clinical review is not performed by this self-study course.

assignment.title: Aging-research protocol synopsis and communication package
deliverables: Two-page specific-aims/protocol synopsis
One-page causal diagram/data-flow figure using conceptual shapes only
Structured evidence table of at least five openly accessible publications/guidelines
Prespecified outcome, estimand, eligibility, time zero, missing-data sensitivity plan and subgroup/transportability limits
Human-subjects/consent/IRB, privacy, safety-monitoring and data-sharing plan
250-word lay summary plus 200-word abstract and one-page limitations statement

rubric.meets: Narrow, important question with explicit population, comparator, outcome and time horizon; no unsupported diagnostic premise.
Design matches question; estimand, time zero, bias/causal assumptions and limits stated.
Outcomes/constructs defined; sample-size logic, missingness and sensitivity plan are appropriate and transparent.
IRB/consent, capacity, privacy, inclusion, safety oversight and data-management constraints addressed.
Claims match evidence, uncertainty and limitations are clear, sources traceable, and files/version plan are reproducible.

assignment.passingRule: 80/100 for formative course completion only; not a credential, patient-care assessment, validated board predictor or substitute for institutional review/faculty supervision.

assessment.format: Open-resource formative practice questions, per-unit applied assignments and a capstone protocol synopsis. No course exam is a board examination.
assessment.rubric: Use the 100-point capstone rubric; each unit formative work must identify evidence, assumptions, limitations and at least one ethical or equity consideration where relevant.
assessment.passingRule: 80/100 on the capstone rubric as a self-study completion target only; scores do not validate competence or forecast passing boards.

mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: One named institutional programme (not multiple DAP institutional variants): an NIH/NIA-supported physician-scientist research pathway in ADRD, frailty and multimorbidity in aging for participating residents from Medicine and Neurology. The MGH page states 12 months, 80% mentored research/20% ambulatory continuity clinic; 12 months extends residency by one year; coursework is individualized and includes required institutional RCR curriculum plus at least one course in biostatistics, grant writing and scientific communication. It also reports ABIM/ABPN approval. The page is not a complete residency curriculum or course/lecture inventory.

unitMap.text: DAP StARR: research-in-residency, aging science and question formation
coveredTopics: R38/StARR purpose; aging-research ecosystem; researchable clinical uncertainty; PICO/PECO; equipoise; mentor and team roles.

unitMap.text: Clinical phenotyping: cognition, frailty, function and multimorbidity
coveredTopics: Cognition/function/frailty operational definitions; informant data; comorbidity and medication confounding; longitudinal phenotype; ascertainment validity.

unitMap.text: Evidence synthesis, biological plausibility and research gap
coveredTopics: Question refinement; evidence hierarchy; systematic search; bias; certainty; replication; evidence gaps.

unitMap.text: Study design and causal inference in aging cohorts
coveredTopics: Cohort/case-control/cross-sectional/trial; target population; estimand; DAGs; time zero; competing risks; pragmatic trials.

unitMap.text: Biostatistics, missingness and longitudinal outcomes
coveredTopics: Descriptive/inferential statistics; confidence intervals; regression; sample size principles; missing data; survival/recurrent events; sensitivity analyses.

unitMap.text: Bioinformatics, biomarkers and reproducibility
coveredTopics: Omics/data provenance; phenotype harmonization; batch effects; train/test leakage; external validation; analytical vs clinical validity; reproducibility.

unitMap.text: Human-subject protections, RCR, dementia consent and safety
coveredTopics: RCR; consent and decision-making capacity; surrogate consent; assent; privacy; vulnerable populations; DSM/DSMB; unanticipated problems; conflicts of interest.

unitMap.text: Trial design, measurement and translational endpoints
coveredTopics: Endpoints; surrogate validity; biomarker qualification; diagnostic accuracy; eligibility; outcome adjudication; harms; protocol versioning.

unitMap.text: Implementation science, health equity and inclusive recruitment
coveredTopics: Reach/adoption/fidelity/sustainability; health disparities; language access; structural barriers; recruitment/retention; transportability.

unitMap.text: Data governance, sharing, privacy and open science
coveredTopics: Data dictionaries; access controls; retention; secure analysis; de-identification; NIH DMS; code/version control; FAIR/open science limits.

unitMap.text: Protocol, grants, scientific communication and peer review
coveredTopics: Specific aims; protocol; grant logic; feasibility; milestones; manuscript/abstract; peer review; figure integrity; stakeholder communication.

unitMap.text: Career development, mentorship, team science and translation
coveredTopics: Mentoring; team science; authorship; research career development; protected time; translational pathways; clinical skill maintenance; dissemination.

topicGaps: No public ledger of finished MGH DAP StARR-only classroom recordings was found. The institutional page describes individualized coursework, monthly career-development meetings and mentoring, but not public media IDs or runtimes; external subject recordings are not official DAP teaching.

Parent internal-medicine and neurology residency clinical decisions, supervised patient care, procedures, case volumes and longitudinal competency remain outside this research supplement; recordings cannot replace accredited training or clinical supervision.

The 36-hour video target is met by the verified external ledger only; it does not mean every unit is covered at equal depth, complete board-blueprint coverage, examination readiness or validated competence.

Unit U12 (career development, mentorship, team science and clinical-skills continuity) lacks a uniquely mapped long-form recording. MGH public pathway statements describe its own mentoring structure but do not furnish teachable recordings; an original clip plan remains.

Units U07, U10 and U11 still need additional source-specific, applied instruction on consent/capacity, privacy/data sharing and grant/communication processes. Existing foundation and summit recordings provide partial exposure, not local IRB, law, NIH award-specific or institutional compliance training.

Board mapping remains a crosswalk to parent ABIM/ABPN domains; neither DAP StARR nor this self-study has an independent exam, accreditation, clinical eligibility or certification. The existing ABIM MOC/LKA and ABPN continuing-certification crosswalk caveats are retained.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: One named institutional programme (not multiple DAP institutional variants): an NIH/NIA-supported physician-scientist research pathway in ADRD, frailty and multimorbidity in aging for participating residents from Medicine and Neurology. The MGH page states 12 months, 80% mentored research/20% ambulatory continuity clinic; 12 months extends residency by one year; coursework is individualized and includes required institutional RCR curriculum plus at least one course in biostatistics, grant writing and scientific communication. It also reports ABIM/ABPN approval. The page is not a complete residency curriculum or course/lecture inventory.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The official directory labels the listing “Medicine / Residency”; the primary MGH programme page names it “MGH DAP StARR” and describes a cross-departmental, one-year research pathway for residents in Medicine and Neurology. It is not a standalone clinical physician specialty or combined IM/Neurology residency. NIH StARR is a research-training funding mechanism. Parent clinical residency, separate board routes and institutional research supplement are distinguished. A separate board exam for DAP StARR was not found.
sourceCaveats: Official MGH program claims are reported as written and have not been independently audited; the public page states ABIM/ABPN approval and funded-opportunity eligibility details.
The MGH directory category “Medicine/Residency” does not make StARR a distinct clinical specialty. The primary page states cross-departmental Medicine/Neurology resident participation.

ABIM blueprint linked here is January 2026 MOC/LKA blueprint; ABPN specifications linked here are for continuing certification. These are not interchangeable with initial certification requirements or the MGH curriculum.
The AAN MCI guideline cited as historical reading was formally retired on 2024-02-10; it is not presented as current clinical guidance.
Publicly viewable means access, not a license to copy or redistribute. All linked cases/videos retain the rights of their owners. No patient-level data or diagnostic images are copied.

Current clinical treatment indications, safety warnings and diagnostic guidance may change after the date checked. Verify current FDA labels and applicable guidelines before any real-world application.
No enrollment, sign-in, paywall bypass or shared browser used; any dynamic, gated or uncertain content is excluded and its gap stated.
No external video topic hours are tagged specialty-specific: the counted IPPCR lectures are foundation-level research methods. Strict track-specific verified duration is zero.

originalClipPlan.title: The first question in an aging-research protocol
objectives: Convert an aging-care observation into a measurable research question.
Choose a defensible design and state an estimand.
Identify measurement, bias, equity, ethics and translation limits.
scriptOutline: Full source-cited script is embedded in pilotScript.
Use only conceptual graphics, not patient data/images.
originalClipPlan.completeScript:
# Pilot: The first question in an aging-research protocol (target 8 minutes; original script)

**Production status: planned script only. No recording, edit, render, upload, or human clinical review is represented as complete.** Use a neutral slide deck with only conceptual shapes and openly linkable text; no patient photographs, scans, records, or fabricated diagnostic images.

**[0:00–0:50 | Opening]**
A research year can begin with a clinical observation, but an observation is not yet a research question. Imagine a clinician who notices that two people with the same chart diagnosis have very different trajectories in memory, daily function, and independence. The goal is not to call one case typical or prove a cause from a story. The goal is to decide what uncertainty can be studied safely and fairly. At Mass General, the DAP StARR programme is a mentored research pathway for residents interested in Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias, frailty, and multimorbidity in aging. It is embedded in residency pathways for participants from Medicine and Neurology; it is not itself a new clinical specialty or a separate board exam. [1]

**[0:50–1:55 | From observation to a measurable question]**
Start by naming the population, exposure or intervention, comparator, outcome, and time window. A broad question such as “Does frailty matter?” is not measurable. A sharper example is: “Among community-dwelling adults aged 70 and older enrolled in a defined memory-clinic cohort, is baseline frailty score associated with change in a prespecified functional measure over two years, after accounting for age, baseline cognition, comorbidity, and follow-up intensity?” This is only an example of question structure—not a claim about a real cohort, a validated instrument, a causal effect, or clinical advice. Define who measures frailty, when it is measured, how missing visits are handled, and what counts as a clinically interpretable change before looking at results.

**[1:55–3:10 | Choose a design that can answer it]**
An observational cohort may describe trajectories and associations, but it cannot remove confounding merely because a regression model includes several variables. A randomized trial can make treatment groups comparable in expectation for the assigned intervention, but it does not guarantee adherence, complete follow-up, representative enrollment, or correct measurement. The NIH clinical-research curriculum emphasizes matching study design to the question, planning the protocol, and protecting participants. [10] Its freely viewable study-design lectures contrast observational and interventional approaches and discuss randomization and design quality. [11] Before selecting a design, write the estimand in plain language: which population, which comparison, which outcome, and when? Specify time zero so that eligibility, exposure assignment, and follow-up start consistently. A causal diagram can make assumptions visible; it cannot prove those assumptions true.

**[3:10–4:35 | Measure cognition without turning a screen into a diagnosis]**
Cognition is not a single number. A brief screening test can identify a need for more assessment, but a positive screen does not by itself establish Alzheimer’s disease or any other etiology. NIA notes that tool selection depends on setting, language, age, demographics, and administrator expertise; positive brief screens need follow-up evaluation. [12] In a study, record the instrument version, language, testing conditions, sensory accommodations, informant source, education context, and functional outcome. Decide whether the outcome represents a symptom, syndrome, biomarker, or clinical diagnosis. These constructs answer different questions. Avoid silently changing an outcome when a protocol amendment or new assay appears.

**[4:35–5:45 | Plan for bias, missingness, and who is represented]**
Older-adult studies can lose participants because of illness, disability, transport, caregiving, institutionalization, or death. If follow-up is less complete for participants with greater impairment, a complete-case analysis may describe a selected group. State likely missingness mechanisms, compare baseline features of retained and lost participants, and pre-specify reasonable sensitivity analyses with a statistician. Do not treat an assumed missing-at-random condition as a fact. Also ask whether recruitment and measurement work for people across languages, cultures, educational backgrounds, and care settings. NIH’s IPPCR includes a health-disparities lecture, and the DAP programme identifies research in aging as its scientific focus. [1] [11]

**[5:45–6:55 | Ethics and feasibility before ambition]**
A clinically important question still needs a feasible protocol and a responsible consent plan. Capacity is decision-specific and should not be inferred solely from age or a diagnosis. Research teams must follow the IRB-approved process, respect the participant’s wishes, involve a legally authorized representative when applicable, and protect privacy. Safety oversight depends on study risk and applicable requirements. NIH’s public course includes research ethics and data-and-safety-monitoring lectures, while DAP StARR participants complete the sponsoring institution’s RCR curriculum. [1] [10] A public lecture cannot substitute for institutional approvals, supervision, or required training.

**[6:55–7:45 | A defensible next step]**
Before the first analysis, write a short protocol synopsis: question; population; eligibility; measures; time zero; comparator; outcome; confounders; sample-size rationale; missing-data plan; participant protections; and limitations. Ask a content expert, methods collaborator, community representative where appropriate, and research oversight office to challenge the assumptions. Keep data access, code, and version history auditable. Do not promise benefit from an exploratory biomarker or confuse a registry entry with proof of efficacy. Verify current treatment indications against current FDA labeling and clinical guidance whenever treatment is relevant; labels can change. [19] [23]

**[7:45–8:10 | Close]**
A strong aging-research question is narrow enough to answer, important enough to matter, and humble enough to show what it cannot establish. DAP StARR’s public description emphasizes mentored research and professional development; this independent learning resource offers background only. It does not confer affiliation, accredited training, clinical competence, licensure, eligibility, or certification. Human clinical review has not been performed. [1]

topicGaps: No public ledger of finished MGH DAP StARR-only classroom recordings was found. The institutional page describes individualized coursework, monthly career-development meetings and mentoring, but not public media IDs or runtimes; external subject recordings are not official DAP teaching.

Parent internal-medicine and neurology residency clinical decisions, supervised patient care, procedures, case volumes and longitudinal competency remain outside this research supplement; recordings cannot replace accredited training or clinical supervision.

The 36-hour video target is met by the verified external ledger only; it does not mean every unit is covered at equal depth, complete board-blueprint coverage, examination readiness or validated competence.

Unit U12 (career development, mentorship, team science and clinical-skills continuity) lacks a uniquely mapped long-form recording. MGH public pathway statements describe its own mentoring structure but do not furnish teachable recordings; an original clip plan remains.

Units U07, U10 and U11 still need additional source-specific, applied instruction on consent/capacity, privacy/data sharing and grant/communication processes. Existing foundation and summit recordings provide partial exposure, not local IRB, law, NIH award-specific or institutional compliance training.

Board mapping remains a crosswalk to parent ABIM/ABPN domains; neither DAP StARR nor this self-study has an independent exam, accreditation, clinical eligibility or certification. The existing ABIM MOC/LKA and ABPN continuing-certification crosswalk caveats are retained.

practiceQuestions.stem: A research team observes that higher baseline frailty scores correlate with faster decline in a memory-clinic cohort. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.text: Frailty causes cognitive decline because the model adjusted for age.
The association is descriptive; residual confounding, selection and measurement error remain plausible.
Frailty is a diagnostic test for Alzheimer’s disease.
An association proves a treatment effect.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Adjustment for age alone does not establish causation. Cohort design supports association subject to design and measurement assumptions.
practiceQuestions.contentStatus: original educational item; not official board content and not a validated predictor of examination performance

practiceQuestions.stem: In an observational aging cohort, participants enter follow-up at different times. What is a key benefit of explicitly defining time zero?

options.text: It guarantees exchangeability.
It aligns eligibility, exposure assignment and follow-up to reduce time-related design bias.
It makes missingness ignorable.
It proves external validity.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A coherent time zero helps avoid misaligned eligibility and follow-up; it cannot remove all confounding or prove validity.
practiceQuestions.contentStatus: original educational item; not official board content and not a validated predictor of examination performance

practiceQuestions.stem: A brief cognitive screen is positive in a fictional patient. Which research/clinical interpretation is appropriate?

options.text: This alone establishes Alzheimer’s disease.
Treat the score as a prompt for more comprehensive evaluation; do not equate screening with etiology.
The result is definitive regardless of language.
No informant or functional history is useful.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NIA cautions that tool choice depends on setting and population, and a positive brief assessment needs follow-up. A screening result is not an etiologic diagnosis.
practiceQuestions.contentStatus: original educational item; not official board content and not a validated predictor of examination performance

practiceQuestions.stem: A randomized trial has substantial loss to follow-up among participants with worsening function. What should the investigators do?

options.text: Assume all missing outcomes equal baseline values.
Report missingness patterns and prespecify justified sensitivity analyses.
Delete the protocol outcome after seeing data.
Claim randomization prevents bias after attrition.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Randomization at baseline does not prevent bias from differential post-randomization missing outcomes. Prespecified analyses and transparent limitations are needed.
practiceQuestions.contentStatus: original educational item; not official board content and not a validated predictor of examination performance

practiceQuestions.stem: A biomarker model performs well in the same dataset used to select features and tune thresholds. What is the largest concern?

options.text: It has been externally validated.
Data leakage/overfitting may inflate apparent performance; independent validation is needed.
It establishes clinical utility.
No further evaluation is needed.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Feature selection and threshold tuning on the evaluation data produce optimistic performance; external validation and intended-use assessment are distinct.
practiceQuestions.contentStatus: original educational item; not official board content and not a validated predictor of examination performance

options.text: Results are necessarily representative of every older adult.
Enrollment/accessibility limits may affect transportability; describe population and plan inclusive recruitment.
Randomization within the sample solves representativeness.
Demographic analysis is prohibited.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Internal validity and external validity are distinct; recruitment constraints may limit generalizability and raise equity questions.

practiceQuestions.stem: An older adult invited to a fictional observational study has a dementia diagnosis. What is the ethically sound first principle?

options.text: Assume incapacity based solely on diagnosis.
Follow IRB-approved, decision-specific capacity and consent processes; respect participant wishes and use an authorized representative if applicable.
Obtain consent from any available relative without checking requirements.
Skip consent because the data are de-identified later.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Age or diagnosis alone does not settle capacity; use applicable institutional, legal and IRB-approved procedures and privacy safeguards.

practiceQuestions.stem: A trial registry lists a completed study with no results posted. What can a learner infer from that record alone?

options.text: The intervention is effective.
The registry verifies efficacy.
The record describes registered study information, but efficacy requires results and critical appraisal.
The trial proves standard of care.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A registry is a study-finding resource, not an endorsement or substitute for results, appraisal, labels and guidelines.

practiceQuestions.stem: A team wants to publish an exploratory association as a validated screening tool. Which evidence is still needed?

options.text: Only a statistically significant p-value.
A prespecified intended use, analytical/clinical validity, independent validation and evaluation of clinical utility.
A press release.
A larger training dataset only.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Discovery, validation and clinical utility are different stages. Exploratory findings should be labeled and independently tested before claims of use.

title: Joint Thoracic and General Surgery Residency
prerequisites: For advanced self-study: medical-school-level anatomy, physiology, pathology, pharmacology, statistics, and supervised clinical education; intended primarily for surgical trainees and clinicians, not the public.
Foundational cardiothoracic videos in the ledger are explicitly from an SCTS Foundation Doctor Academy and are introductory; they are not asserted to match U.S. residency depth.
Required tools: current ABS SCORE general-surgery curriculum, current ACGME/board documents, and local institutional protocols.
objectives: Distinguish a 4+3 joint pathway from integrated I-6 and independent cardiothoracic pathways and state the limits of public programme/board evidence.
Use a structured differential, staging and multidisciplinary reasoning approach to thoracic surgical problems without converting a video or image into a clinical recommendation.
Describe lung cancer evaluation, screening evidence, staging logic, and surgical candidacy as disease resectability, physiological operability, and patient goals—not as a single image finding.
Reason through pleural disease, chest trauma, aortic/cardiac conditions, perioperative risk, postoperative complications, ICU escalation, safety, and quality improvement.
Map the learning portfolio to public ABS/ABTS and ACGME domains while identifying dated, non-U.S., incomplete, or inaccessible resources.

boardNames: American Board of Surgery (ABS)
American Board of Thoracic Surgery (ABTS)
medical.boardStatus: This is a real combined clinical physician training pathway. The ACGME identifies a Joint General Surgery/Thoracic Surgery (4+3) pathway; successful training may lead to eligibility to seek certification by both the ABS and ABTS, not a combined joint-board credential. The boards maintain distinct certification processes/exams. Certification is not conferred by this course.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: The ACGME pathway description states that approved seven-year 4+3 education/training leads to eligibility for certification in both general surgery and thoracic surgery, after prior approval by the Surgery and Thoracic Surgery Review Committees. Program-specific approval, institution pairing, trainee eligibility, completion of all current requirements, and actual eligibility remain subject to the ACGME, ABS, ABTS, and program director; this independent course cannot establish them or guarantee certification. Verify current individual requirements directly with ABS/ABTS before relying on any prior rule.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The packet names two exact institutional variants (BWH and MGH) under the broader Mass General Brigham directory; they are retained separately, not collapsed into one generic directory result. Official ACGME and TSDA sources define this as an actual combined clinical 4+3 physician-training pathway, distinct from the six-year integrated cardiothoracic pathway and the traditional post-general-surgery pathway. This is not a research/non-physician track and is not merely a board-directory category. ACGME/TSDA establish the general dual-board pathway, but public evidence reviewed here does not independently resolve every current institutional pairing, applicant eligibility, or trainees' outcomes. No clinical rotations, procedural privileges, patient/case volume, institutional enrollment, or Harvard faculty access are offered by this independent school.
sourceCaveats: The institutional pages/program directory entries identify named BWH and MGH joint programmes, but are not public syllabi; public material reviewed does not expose complete local rotations, operative case logs, quiz sets, exact lecture hours, current applicant eligibility, or outcomes.

The ACGME describes prior approval and dual-board eligibility for a 4+3 pathway; ABS/ABTS qualifications remain subject to each board's current rules. The separate boards do not create a joint certification. Verify current program-specific pairing with ACGME and the program director.

The 36-hour floor is not met by verified resources here. Counted 15.9161 hours are unique public SCTS cardiothoracic foundation lectures; they remain foundation-category hours and are not reclassified as advanced specialty lectures. Specialty-specific and supplemental hour counts are zero in the strictly verified ledger. Six candidate public videos with unresolved runtimes are listed but excluded.

SCTS is a UK professional society and its academy targets foundation doctors; UK scope, language, standards and depth require U.S. board-curriculum cross-check. The videos provide no proof of U.S. licensure or competence.
Public video's free-to-view status is not a copyright licence; links only. No third-party media is embedded or copied.

Clinical case use is limited to links. TCIA is an authentic repository-described de-identifying archive: LIDC-IDRI has incomplete diagnostic/pathology truth and the DICOM annotation derivative represents only selected nodules. Both datasets are CC BY 3.0 with DOI attribution and usage requirements. Do not attempt to identify participants; do not rehost/copy patient images or records.

No human clinical review was performed. Clinical guidance dates can change; verify at point of use. Course is not affiliated with Harvard, BWH, MGH, ACGME, ABS, ABTS, TSDA or SCTS and grants no accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, procedural competence, certification, patient-care authorization or pass guarantee.
